#6643. As Podcasters Become Cultural Juggernauts, Brands Should Probably Tune In

On a recent episode of Mary Beth Barone and Benito Skinner’s podcast, Ride, the hosts paused their conversation to talk about each other’s ’fits. “What is this kinda top?” Skinner asks, to which Barone replies declaring it vintage Miu Miu. Skinner goes on to cosplay an OOTD video, running through his full outfit: society archive T-shirt “vintage, of course”, vintage Ralph Lauren Polo shorts, and flip flops by The Row. Ride is not a fashion podcast with a capital-F, but this moment underscores why podcasts today — now largely streamed as videos — are becoming important platforms for fashion.

Brands are starting to take note. Skinner regularly sits front row at Prada, and has shot campaigns or content for Tory Burch, J.Crew and Ralph Lauren. Barone has attended the Tory Burch show for the last three seasons. And on the podcast, their brand deals include workout label Tonal, hair brand K18, and Bobbi Brown’s Jones Road.

And it’s not just Ride. During the Spring/Summer 2027 men’s and women’s seasons, podcasters were a front row fixture, including Therapuss’s Jake Shane at Calvin Klein and Dior Men, In Your Dreams host Owen Thiele at Louis Vuitton, and How Long Gone host Chris Black, who’s become a regular at Copenhagen Fashion Week, sometimes alongside co-host Jason Stewart.

In Your Dreams host and Adults star Owen Thiele attended Louis Vuitton SS27 in September.

It makes sense. The global podcast industry generated an estimated $9.2 billion in sales last year, up 23% versus 2024, largely based on a surge in video content, per Bloomberg. Apple and Spotify were once the primary podcasting platforms, but now major streamers including Netflix, Hulu, Tubi, and Disney+ are entering the space. Roughly 81% of weekly podcast listeners now tune into video, either on streaming platforms or YouTube. Video helps podcasters grow their audience: in the age of clipping, many young people will discover new podcasters after seeing the show clipped on TikTok or Reels.

“Over the last three years, the definition of a podcast has changed entirely,” says Rebecca Steinberg, creator agent at United Talent Agency (UTA), who represents Therapuss with Shane, Good Guys with Josh Peck and Ben Soffer, among others. “The way audiences consume podcasts has shifted, and by extension, so has the way the industry defines and categorizes the format.”

With more podcasts signing streaming deals and launching video and live events, the medium is becoming more visual, driving its growth and creating an opportunity for fashion to tap in. But of course, there’s a balance to strike. As these beloved talents build major cultural resonance, it’s important they maintain the credibility and community they’ve cultivated.

The podcast ad read (where the host reads pre-records ads for the break) is the most traditional way for brands to tap into the market. And for the most beloved of podcasters, these reads, often featuring an in-joke or a tongue-in-cheek admission, can be compelling on their own. (In fact, podcast ads deliver the highest ad performance of any brand channel.) “Because people choose to consume podcasts [rather than being bombarded with content on the feed], their recommendations carry more weight,” Steinberg says. “Podcast and creator audiences are incredibly sticky, and that trust creates a unique opportunity for brands to reach potential buyers.”

“Podcasters’ cultural power has grown significantly in recent years,” says Marissa Hurwitz, talent agent at WME, who represents Ride’s Skinner and Barone, alongside other podcasters like Paige DeSorbo (Giggly Squad), Tinx (It’s Me, Tinx), Alaina Urquhart and Ashleigh Kelley (Morbid), Bailey Sarian (Dark History), and Rayna Greenberg and Ashley Hesseltine (Girls Gotta Eat). “It was previously a side door for talents while they worked on other projects. But now, podcasting is the main event. They’ve gone from being niche voices to [the talents] audiences trust the most.”

A.J. Leone is a UTA creators agent who’s worked in the podcast space for nine years. His client roster includes Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers (Las Culturistas), Emma Chamberlain (Anything Goes), Jonathan Van Ness (Getting Better), and Brittany Broski (The Broski Report and Royal Court). “Brands of all kinds want to tap into podcasts today because of the long-form format where the audience is captivated,” he says. “The podcast audience is not just passively scrolling on TikTok. They’re clicking play on YouTube, on their podcast player, on Netflix, and they’re choosing to listen or watch for 45-60 minutes. As a result, a brand partnership that’s part of a podcast feels more authentic; when listening, people feel like they’re on FaceTime with a friend.”

Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers of Las Culturistas hosted their fifth Culture Awards in May of this year. The event was broadcasted by Bravo and Peacock.

As our feeds become increasingly filled with fleeting, transitory connections, and taste continues to convert into a valued commodity, podcasters provide a trusted barometer on what culture people should tune into — from books to movies to songs — or they function as a trusty friend, with whom audiences share in-jokes and a specific vernacular that feels familiar each time they listen. Some have even gone as far as to conceive tongue-in-cheek, IRL award ceremonies, from the Las Culturistas Culture Awards to How Long Gone’s The Goneies, which launched this year, awarding Barone as It-girl of the Year, signifying their role as arbiters of taste, even if it’s esoteric.

So, as the value of taste rises, and audiences seek intellectual influencers who enrich their knowledge rather than serve them slop, podcasters are primed to capture brand marketing revenue from traditional creators.

Mary Beth Barone regularly attends the Tory Burch show at NYFW.

“Established podcasters should be understood as brands in their own right, and an awards show is the clearest sign of that. It’s not a side project, it’s the brand’s IP expanding into the exact territory traditional cultural figures already operate in,” says Parisa Parmar, strategist at culture and entertainment marketing agency Attachment. “Sustained conversation on relevant topics positions a host as a cultural barometer over time, rather than a one-off voice. There’s a genuine appetite for an unfiltered point of view, and it’s fueling what is known as the ‘credibility economy’, where having a genuine take is a form of social power or capital.”

Podcaster relatability is what moves the needle. “Culturally, we have a strange relationship with expertise. We want those people who don’t seem like they’re talking down to us,” says Annie Corser, pop culture analyst at Stylus. “Podcasters have some more inbuilt credibility, so we allow them to be tastemakers, it’s different to other types of media like film or TV in that it is by and large non-fiction. So we’re going there for information.”

This is compelling for partners, adds WME’s Hurwitz. “You’re really getting to work with people who haven’t just necessarily also grown up and been like, ‘I want to be a star,’” she says. “It’s people who have these really fascinating niche interests that they use their podcasts to share.”

The visual nature of modern podcasts is changing how podcasters work with brands, experts agree. Las Culturistas — the growing pop culture podcast hosted by Yang and Rogers — signed a new deal with Disney+ and Hulu on October 15, to stream the pod on both platforms. Leaning into the visual side of the show, the duo launched a new video set over the summer, which has allowed for more product placements and brand interactions, says UTA agent Leone. “Fashion hasn’t tapped into the podcast space as significantly as other categories,” he adds. “But it’s only a matter of time, especially with the added visual component.”

Shane — who is increasingly booking major talent interviews — signed a deal with Netflix in January to stream his episodes on the platform. “Bringing Therapuss to Netflix was one inflection point that signaled platforms traditionally associated with TV and film see real value in licensing and distributing creator-produced shows that originated on social and audio platforms,” Steinberg says. “Hollywood is seeing that these creators are the new frontier of entertainment — backing them with bigger budgets, new distribution, and the ability to story tell on a different stage.”

Therapuss host Jake Shane attended Calvin Klein SS27; he also signed a major deal with Alo in the summer, as brands begin to understand the power of his hyper-engaged community.

This summer, Alo tapped Shane as an ambassador, launching a workout series with him on the Alo app, after he spent three years training at the Alo Wellness Club in LA (and posting the difficult journey). “It’s clear to the audience that there is a true relationship there, and I think the customer can just feel it and see it, and that’s why they connect with the brand more organically,” said Alo CEO Benedetta Petruzzo after the launch.

Podcasters today are such prominent cultural figures that many of them are already being styled and photographed for events, Hurwitz says. “The audiences are so loyal and engaged in a way that translates to real purchasing power. People with a podcast business like Benito, Mary Beth, Hannah Berner, Paige Desorbo, Tinx, you see all of them showing up at these fashion week events because fans truly want to see where they’re going, what they’re wearing, who they’re wearing, and how can they get their hands on it.”

The evolution of podcast video is “irrefutably big”, Stylus’s Corser says. But the next avenue for growth, she shares, is IRL podcast recordings and events, presenting more brand activation opportunities.

Barone and Skinner completed a Ride live tour last year, where they held IRL versions of the podcast across the US and Europe in sold-out venues. People turned up in T-shirts with in-jokes from the pod, Hurwitz says. “Baronies” are also increasingly staging their own IRL events, having connected via Instagram fan accounts and group chats, presenting a hyper-engaged audience for brands to tap into via sponsorship. “People have chosen to go and see people that they think are friends, and then the assumption is these friends of mine will have chosen brands really carefully, so I’ll pay attention to them,” Corser says. “People want brands to help them get out of the house.”

Owen Thiele of In Your Dreams and Benito Skinner of Ride at the WYouth launch in Los Angeles.

There are more and more brands that want to be part of that real-life podcast moment, says Leone. Podcaster Heather McMahan of Absolutely Not even staged a live event on a cruise. “Her fans are willing not just to go on the road with her, but are willing to go on a boat and do a whole cruise with her,” he adds. “So it’s really the community that they build.”

Of course, the brands showing up on video or at live events need to align with the podcasters’ actual tastes. “One of the things that we really focus on at WME is trying to super serve [the audience] and ensure that we’re protective of the podcaster,” talent agent Hurwitz says. Whether it’s on the pod or off, “we never want to do anything with the brand that would jeopardize the incredible relationship and community that they’ve built with the audience.”

Hurwitz points to a recent episode of Ride as an example of how to work with brands that fit. “One ad was for Squarespace, which Mary Beth used to build her website,” she explains. “Another of the ads was for Nocd, so Benny spoke about the fact he was diagnosed with OCD. It’s about aligning partnerships with who they are as people.”

Alignment is “the biggest thing”, Steinberg concurs. “Brands need to let podcasters talk about a product in their own voice, and trust that they know their audience best and what will be entertaining, informative and actually resonate. If a brand is overly prescriptive about the creative, it can be difficult because there’s going to be misalignment. Creators have a direct relationship with their audience, and they know what works.”

Live events allow brands to be part of a podcast community without interrupting the pod during an ad break. “Meaningful alignment means going where the fans already gather outside the show itself, and adding something rather than inserting something,” Parmar says. “That might mean a live event built around the podcast’s community rather than its content, a physical product collaboration that only makes sense because of who the host is, or simply showing up to genuinely help solve a problem that community already has.”

Based on their growing cultural power, podcast talents are expanding their careers across different fields, presenting more opportunities as they grow. Yang (who was previously a regular on Saturday Night Live) is currently starring in Oh, Mary! on Broadway, Thiele acts in TV series Adults, while Skinner wrote and starred in series Overcompensating on Prime, which also features Barone and is currently filming season two. The podcast is a crucial platform for talents to build a closer community, boosting their external projects, Hurwitz says. “Now, we can take a podcast business and build it into many other areas. Whether that is TV, is it a book? Is it a tour? Is it a venture deal? Is it more brand deals? That’s really helped differentiate some of the podcasters we represent.”

#6641. The 15 Best Chelsea Boots for Men in 2026: Never Go Out of Style

The best Chelsea boots for men are trend-proof in a way that'll make you breathe a sigh of relief. Especially right now, when menswear feels like a WWE Royal Rumble, where anything goes and trends pile up like bodies in and out of the ring. But there, floating confidently above everything, is the trustworthy Chelsea boot.

If we had to make an educated guess as to why the Chelsea boot has stuck around for so long? Good design is good design. The slip-on simplicity, the sharp silhouette, the unadorned, uncomplicated details—the pared-back design makes it highly adaptable to any wardrobe and occasion, trends be damned. So don't be ashamed to cash in on a fleeting fad, but when it comes time for you to do some spring cleaning, we'd advise against letting go of a pair of Chelseas.

We've rounded up 15 of the best Chelsea boots out there, from hardwearing stompers to exquisite stunners, $200 steals to $1,500 beauties. Finding the perfect pair can be hard—but pulling them on? Easy.

Ask us what Chelsea boot you should get, regardless of price, and we'll point to the R.M. Williams Turnout boot, because it does so many things right that the competition can't. Off the bat, it’s a real stunner. The silhouette is sleek and chiseled, timeless and fashion forward. The leather is perfectly suited for a shine and polish to attend any black tie event, but takes on a handsome patina when worn hard. Plus, the quality is fantastic. The wholecut leather uppers are shaped as a single piece of cowhide rather than several panels stitched together, resulting in a shoe that’s as pretty as it is durable. With Goodyear-welted construction for easy peasy resoling, you’ll have these Aussie-born boots for well over a decade.

How does a boot originally built for Down Under cowboys manage to be the best-looking dress boot and hardest-wearing boot at the same time? Hard to say. The only drawback of the R.M. Williams Heritage Craftsman Chelsea is the price. But considering everything it can do—and how long it'll last—the math makes sense.

For the budget conscious/the dude looking for his first pair of “nice” Chelsea boots, my answer is easy: Beckett Simonon. Menswear bros might scoff at a web-only DTC clothing brand, but unlike the other brands with infinite marketing budgets looking to “disrupt the entire industry”, Beckett Simonon seems content with making great shoes at a great price, without all the soulless millennial pandering. The Bolton, a slick sleek, true-to-form  Chelsea boot, is just the poster child for the brand’s modus operandi. It uses full-grain Italian calfskin, which is lined with Vachetta leather, stitched by master shoemakers in Columbia using a Blake stitch construction.

In other words, it’s a Chelsea boot with A-list looks, Northamptonshire-style pedigree, and a price that’s at least half of the competition. But if there’s one thing that will stop most people from buying a pair immediately is, well, you can’t get them immediately. Each pair is made to order, which means you’ll have to wait a month or two to get yours. But you know what they say: patience is a virtue.

Some Chelsea boots lean heavily into their rockstar appeal, while others skew utilitarian, expressly designed to protect you from the elements. Then there, however, are the rare pairs that gracefully straddle the line between. Enter the other Australian boot: Blundstone. Those tough leather uppers might not be monsoon-ready, but on days when you just need to jump a few puddles en route to work, the whole package is the slickest way to ensure your socks stay dry without compromising your fit.

Tired Bushwick memes aside, Blunnies are truly good looking boots built like a tank. They can take a real whooping and still show up for their 5 a.m. shift behind the espresso machine, ready for more. They’re a boot you don’t have to feel precious about, and the de facto kicks to wear when the weather forecast just says “shitty.” They look great with vintage jeans, a pair of Dickies, cargo pants, and chinos—though, in our humble opinion, they don't belong anywhere with a dress code (explicit or implied).

Hedi Slimane’s legacy at Saint Laurent was all skinny jeans, razor-sharp suits, and rockstar Chelsea boots. The look he cooked up over a decade ago has come back again, with guys dubbing themselves Hedi Boys looking to recreate the magic. One glance at boots like these, and you understand why. A leading man gleam and a stacked Cuban heel mean these boots by themselves could headline Coachella. The only update: a very right-now edginess (literally) at the toe. Whether or not the rumored skinny jeans comeback arrives, these are the boots to wear when you want all eyes on you.

Astorflex has long been one of the best value propositions in the shoe space. The Tuscan vegetable-tanned leather and multigenerational craftsmanship alone should be worth more than what you'll actually pay. But value doesn't equate to style. Thankfully, the Bitflex has that in spades. Not too pointy and not totally bulbous, the shape splits the difference masterfully and looks great paired with any kind of pants. Plus, the cushioned crepe sole plays down the dressy factor while adding a ton of comfort straight out of the box.

Unlike other crepe-soled boots more famous than these—ahem—these don’t feel suspiciously soft, despite their extremely comfortable feel. In my experience, Astorflex boots maintain great arch support and mold to your feet, but also are built up enough to provide some noticeable ankle support. This is certainly the most casual Chelsea boot here, so don’t even think of trying to wear these to your friend’s wedding. You’re not “doing something”, you’re being disrespectful.

If you think of Red Wing, it's the brand’s iconic 6-inch moc toe boots you’re probably imagining. But the Minnesotan boot makers can do more than turn out jobsite-endorsed footwear. Introduced in the 1990s, Red Wing’s Chelseas were made for ranchers who wanted something durable enough for the farm, but easy enough to nap in. They’re a happy middle ground between a high-shine European Chelsea like the R.M. Williams and the woodsy Blundstones.

That means you get Goodyear-welted construction and built-to-stroll rubber outsoles topped by Hawthorne Muleskinner roughout suede. The texture is “rugged handyman,” but the dusty tan and dark brown color can hold down a coffee date-worthy fit. White tees and white jeans? Sure. Nice pants and a knit sweater or polo? Absolutely. Wranglers and a Stetson. Of course.

Morjas is best known for loafers worn by everyone from Wall Street bros to Greenpoint baristas. Now the Swedish shoemakers are coming for your ankles with a Chelsea boot. If you’ve already graduated from Chelsea Boots 101 by having a classic black or brown calf-leather pair in your closet, consider these brown suede beauties for next semester.

They're fully leather-lined but require absolutely zero break-in time, thanks to a studded rubber sole that feels like walking on a cloud... if clouds had traction. Style-wise, they walk the line (pun intended) between office-ready and weekend cool—equally dialed in when paired with a crisp white dress shirt beneath unforgiving Monday-morning fluorescents or some linen pants while you sip a doppia espresso in Florence.

You already know what that yellow stitching means. Dr. Martens’ chunky, iconic boots bring an EVA insole and the brand's patented oil- and slip-resistant AirWair sole to the water-resistant oiled leather. Add a pull tab for easy entry, and the only thing easier than slipping them on is adding them to cart when you realize they’re on sale.

By cutting out the middleman and selling direct-to-consumer, Meermin offers handsome, Goodyear-welted dress shoes—all made from leather with absurdly tony provenances—for well below what the other guys charge. You can’t go wrong with any of the brand’s boots, but a mocha-hued suede Chelsea looks especially killer in the fall.

Blundstones again, you say? Well, yes. But this pair has a leather lining and plusher sole, which make them both more comfortable and longer lasting, if for a slightly higher price.

From the rugged to the refined. Chelsea boots are named after London's affluent Chelsea neighbourhood, and this model from British quality shoemakers Crockett & Jones' lives up to that name perhaps more than any on this list.

The Spanish shoe-whisperers at Camper fly a little under the radar compared to their British counterparts, but their Chelsea boots offer just as much swaggering rock-god energy as any other pair on this list. Thanks to a cushy OrthoLite footbed, though, you can wear ‘em long after Mick Jagger takes his final bow.

The chatter about Our Legacy's Camion boots never seems to end. That handsome silhouette, the '90s-esque square toe, and the slick side zip make these a modern-day classic.

Viberg makes boots on steroids in its family-owned Canadian factory, turning out museum-worthy footwear designed to stomp through the worst the world—or the ground, at least—has to offer. These Chelseas are cut from a single piece of waxed leather, like a Barbour jacket for your feet.

NYC-based 3sixteen has been on an absolute footwear tear lately—first with its slick Saucony collab, and now with a lug-soled Chelsea boot that stands on business. The whole shoe smashes together slightly disparate details—an elegant tobacco-colored suede, a workmanlike wedge lugged sole, an skyscraper-height ankle—that add up to something fresh in the normally staid world of Chelsea boots. And if you’ve ever broken in a pair of 3sixteen’s top-tier jeans, you already know: things only get better as you put in the steps.

Chelsea boots have always looked cool—anywhere, on anyone, at any time. They were invented in the 1800s, but won their cultural cred later: the Beatles gave them a massive co-sign in the ’60s, then Hedi Slimane anchored his Saint Laurent rocker suits with them while rappers stacked their denim on top of Chelsea boots during the 2010s.

Which goes to show that Chelsea boots work with damn near anything in your closet, from your favorite Levi’s to baggy chinos to louche suits—even crew socks and shorts, depending on the boots and your taste for channeling some Pacific Northwest crunchiness. For more, check out our guide on how to wear Chelsea boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6640. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6639. The New Moon in Scorpio Has Arrived—Here’s What It Means for Every Star Sign

The New Moon in Scorpio occurs on November 9. The second New Moon of autumn marks the start of a fresh lunar cycle, calling on us to manifest with intention. It is a moment for deep contemplation and renewal, anchored in Scorpio’s penetrating, introspective terrain. Step by step, we are learning to step into our power by honoring our most authentic, self-sufficient selves—regardless of the roadblocks standing in our way.

“The New Moon in Scorpio represents an intimate kind of beginning,” Bri Luna, founder of The Hoodwitch and author of Sex Magic For Dummies, explains. “Scorpio brings us into contact with sex, death, sorrow, and the appetites we keep private. Under this Moon, we may recognize how much of ourselves we’ve concealed to preserve a relationship or hold on to a life we’ve outgrown. There can be grief in admitting that, but also a renewed thirst for living. We can still want something deeply, even after disappointment.”

Internally, we are called to reshape and revitalize our daily lives. The urge to evolve into a more grounded, radiant version of ourselves is palpable. The rebirth we are undergoing invites us to shed old layers: like the metamorphosis from chrysalis to butterfly, real transformation takes patience before we can truly take flight.

Action-oriented Mars, the traditional ruler of Scorpio, squares this New Moon. The bold fire of Mars in Leo pushes us to take decisive steps toward fulfilling our longings. The catch? Mars entered its pre-retrograde shadow on November 5 (gearing up to station retrograde on January 10), which means forward momentum may feel sluggish. We are also navigating five concurrent planetary retrogrades: Mercury in Scorpio clouding choices, Venus in Libra recalibrating relationships, Saturn in Aries testing commitments, Uranus in Gemini upending collective viewpoints, and Neptune in Aries reframing our ideals. Hesitation and fog are natural under this sky, but they provide fertile ground to pause and reassess. Resist the urge to rush. Meditate on what your spirit actually needs by tuning into gut-level intuition.

Read your New Moon in Scorpio horoscope below.

Living well remains the best revenge, especially when you have no interest in petty disputes. If you find yourself watching karmic loops play out for others, there’s no need to get your hands dirty. What goes around comes around—step back, protect your peace, and focus on your own lane.

People are naturally drawn to your warmth and charm right now. With the lunation stirring up connections from the past, present, and future, your instinct is to nurture genuine camaraderie. Just make sure you aren't spreading your emotional bandwidth too thin; be discerning about who gets a front-row seat to your life.

The energy you’ve been pouring into others needs to be directed back inward. Before comparing your progress to what everyone else is doing, reclaim your focus. Clarify your own immediate priorities and creative sparks—once you reconnect with what drives you, you’ll move forward without second-guessing yourself.

Vulnerability can feel daunting, especially when scars from past connections linger. While defining a partnership or opening up emotionally might bring up old anxieties, remember that every dynamic is unique. Don’t let former heartaches dictate current possibilities; take intimacy at a pace that feels genuinely safe.

Retreating to your sanctuary is the best way to ride out external noise until the dust settles. You’re in the mood to guard your energy and keep your inner circle close and calm. Filter out anything that drains your vitality, prioritizing quiet restorative rituals that reinforce your peace of mind.

Conversations may feel unusually fraught or prone to misinterpretation right now. If others are projecting their stress or deflecting accountability, verbal sparring won’t help. Opt for clarity, brevity, and space—sometimes putting your thoughts into a carefully considered note is far more effective than an off-the-cuff debate.

Reframing your financial habits is front and center under this lunation. Stepping away from a scarcity mindset is the first step toward unlocking sustainable earning power and security. Transforming how you manage and value your resources takes time; don’t hesitate to seek sound advice from trusted professionals to sharpen your strategy.

We are all creatures of habit—even you. Take an honest look at recurring patterns that have outlived their purpose. Breaking generational or personal cycles can feel intense, but it is deeply liberating. Use this New Moon in your sign to take that first decisive step toward personal reinvention; real momentum will follow.

A sudden moment of clarity may reveal someone’s true motives, dislodging assumptions you’ve held for a while. If you previously gave people the benefit of the doubt at the expense of your gut instincts, don’t dwell on regret. Take the revelation as valuable data to better curate who earned your trust moving forward.

Be selective about the alliances you form right now. Aligning with colleagues or partners who aren’t on your wavelength will only complicate your path, particularly if conflicting agendas create unnecessary friction. Do your due diligence and ensure that potential collaborators are as dependable, honest, and hardworking as you are.

Clarifying long-term career benchmarks may feel like a moving target amid so much retrograde motion. The secret is not to lose faith in your underlying vision just because the timeline shifts. Stay committed to your craft; opportunities often resurface in unexpected and far more fitting ways once the celestial fog clears.

Releasing rigid expectations opens the door to expansive intellectual and philosophical shifts. You might find yourself revisiting core beliefs from earlier in life with a fresh, more forgiving perspective. True growth requires staying adaptable rather than digging your heels in—there is power in doing a complete 180 when new insight demands it.

#6636. How to Avoid Sports Injuries in Your 30s, 40s, and Beyond

At 38 years old, I’ve been fortunate enough to go most of my life without being bothered by sports injuries, despite being consistently and competitively active for the better part of three decades. On the soccer field, I’ve played on and off at club level since primary school. (I’m currently holding it down as a winger on my local club’s 30+ “seniors” team.)

Meanwhile, as a health journalist and all-around enthusiastic exerciser, I’ve thrown myself at countless physical challenges—mostly for fun, sometimes to help pay the rent. Marathons, trail races, triathlons, 24-hour relays, mud runs, obstacle course races, Hyrox—you name it, I was probably obsessed with it for a time. And through it all, the only injury I ever incurred was a torn meniscus (the undignified result of attempting a wildly above-my-paygrade basketball dunk on a charitably lowered rim, at a promotional event). If only the surgeon could have extracted the memory of that day along with the frayed connective tissue he removed from my knee. I’m pretty sure I was wearing jeans, too.

All of this to say, everything was smooth sailing for a very long time, until it suddenly wasn’t. Somewhere around the age of 35, for reasons beyond my comprehension at the time, the wheels started to come off the bus. First, a stress fracture to my foot. I noticed it one night in bed and couldn’t tell you when it happened. Regardless, it put me in a boot for three months.

Next, a torn hamstring during a routine game of pick-up football, making the same run I’d made so many times before. I thought I’d just pulled it, so I kept playing, which of course only made it worse. That decision cost me six months. Then a strained calf muscle at a gentle session of run club. And, finally, shin splints. I don’t even remember how many months that one took me out for, but it felt like forever.

This barrage of sports injuries—all sustained within a roughly two-year period—was unrelenting, each overlapping pang seemingly passing the baton to the next. Needless to say, I was miserable. And the worst part was that I couldn’t understand why this was happening to me. I had been maintaining the same activity level, same diet, same supplements, and the same sleeping habits.

You always hear people talking half-jokingly about how getting older takes its toll on the body. But nothing really prepares you for that moment when you start to actually experience it for yourself. It’s existential. Brutal. Depressing, honestly. Sometimes the best way to deal with these spiral-inducing moments is to simply talk to other people dealing with the same thing. So I recently asked my, er, seasoned soccer team’s group chat: What do you do to avoid and manage sports injuries as you get older?

Kevin, 40, chimes in first: “There’s no avoiding, mate. Just managing.”

“Funnily enough, I’ve actually started doing yoga, which has been great for mobility and stretching out my lower back,” writes Chris, 35, who battles with a recurring quadratus lumborum (QL) issue. “I was always a bit hesitant to give it a go—not because I didn't think it would help, but because I couldn't get past the fact that I'd essentially be following a similar exercise plan to my mum! I think that’s been one of the bigger adjustments as I’ve gotten older: accepting that looking after your body sometimes means doing things you might have previously associated with an entirely different generation.”

“For me, I think the most important thing is to keep going in general,” adds Brian, who recently turned 42. “I remember when I was around 20 years old, my manager at the time, who was in his late 30s and retired from playing, was doing some running on his own before the team training session started. The lads were joking and teasing him about making a comeback, but I remember him saying, ‘If you stop moving at my age, you won't be able to start again.’ I think that’s good advice.”

In some way, I suppose it’s comforting to know that this is something we all have to deal with, whether you’re a Sunday league bench warmer or in contention for the Ballon d’Or. "With age, there’s just a higher incidence of soft-tissue injuries as your muscles lose strength and elasticity,” says Dr. Brian Forsythe, a sports medicine surgeon, associate professor at Rush University Medical Center, and recreational soccer player himself. According to Forsythe, who also serves as head orthopedic officer for MLS team Chicago Fire FC and president of the Professional Soccer Physicians Society, over time athletes across the skill spectrum will ultimately begin running into the same injuries.

You may not be able to halt the inevitable march of time, but there are certainly ways to minimize and slow its toll on your body. This requires some work but could ultimately be the difference between hanging up your boots and kicking on for another 10, 20, or even 30 years.

“It's up to you to take some responsibility,” Forsythe says. “Think about the lifestyle you had when you were 17 or 18—how you took care of your body and what you looked like. Then look in the mirror and ask yourself, ‘How much of my life now resembles what it was then?’ If you’re going out and having a few pints, understand that that inhibits your recovery and decreases protein synthesis. If you’re overweight, that has effects beyond just not looking great in your clothes. It’s increased joint load, increased rotational torque. You’re more likely to get injured. So you have to set realistic expectations of what your body is capable of doing. But you can definitely still do a lot.”

If you’re not ready to call time just yet, here are a couple of strategies you can start implementing today, courtesy of Forsythe and a handful of other experts.

“Number one, and it should be obvious, is just general conditioning,” says Forsythe. Being a slightly less sedentary human being during the work week means you won’t send your body into total shock when you decide to get going over the weekend.

“A lot of injuries come from that mismatch between what we do all week and the intensity we demand from our bodies on the weekend,” says sports medicine physician Dr. Alex McDonald. As Dr. James B. Chen, orthopedic surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center, puts it: “The biggest risk isn't necessarily your age, but your schedule.”

“When you think about playing in your teens and twenties, you were probably close to your ideal body weight,” says Forsythe. Ideal body weight, or IBW, refers to the weight at which your body is able to function most efficiently and without a heightened risk of injury. “All of the forces across your joints are multiplied almost exponentially with additional pounds on your frame,” says Forsythe. For example, “the force across your knee can be up to six times your body weight.”

“If you've ever been overweight and you climb up and down stairs and notice that the front of your knee hurts, that's because of those increased pressures and forces,” adds Forsythe.

Jogging a couple of miles a week may help you get through your Sunday workout our pick-up game, but it’s not doing anything to prevent in-the-moment injuries. To do that, you have to train the way you play—whatever game that is. “It's changes of direction," says Forsythe. It's rapid acceleration and deceleration. It's pivoting, twisting, turning.” Basically, bring back whatever drills you used to do on your sports team when you were younger, and adjust them for the demands of the sport you currently play.

No matter how frequently and comprehensively you train, a complete warm-up before any big athletic event is a non-negotiable. "It helps dramatically, which is why you'll always see professionals warm up for 30-45 minutes before a match,” says Forsythe. When it comes to soccer, FIFA actually has developed a warm-up program, called FIFA ll+, specifically for injury prevention. “It’s a free routine that only takes about 20 minutes, and includes running drills plus strength, balance, and landing exercises such as Nordic hamstring curls and single-leg balance work,” says McDonald. “It’s been shown to cut injuries by about a third, but it needs to be done at least twice a week—ideally three or four times a week—to really reduce the risk of injury.”

Stretching after your warm-up is important, too, but just be careful not to overdo it. “If you stretch too aggressively, you can actually predispose yourself to muscle tendon injuries,” says Forsythe. “First warm up, and then stretch out within your range of comfort. But right before a game is not the time to all of a sudden correct tight hamstrings.”

Often, being sidelined by an injury can be more painful than the injury itself, causing guys to get back out there earlier than they probably should. “A common issue that I see is when someone sustains a minor sprain or strain, and they return to sport-specific activity too early,” says Chen, “which can result in either worsening the injury or even picking up a secondary injury.” As annoying as it might be to sit out for 2 or 3 weeks with a strained hamstring, turning that into a tear will bench you for far longer. Believe me.

Playing sports in your 30s, 40s, and beyond also means coming to grips with your body’s increasing need for routine recovery between training sessions and games. "You have to recognize that your body needs more time to recover,” says Forsythe. You may have great cardiovascular fitness and feel ready to play on consecutive days, but your muscles and connective tissues need time to bounce back. “It’s important to respect fatigue, and ensure proper recovery after games or training,” says McDonald.

To be fair, this is universally sound guidance regardless of age. But it's advice that tends to take decades to sink in. “I think that one of the key advantages of playing as you get older is that you know your body better in your 30s and 40s,” Brian’s response concluded. “You understand what it's saying to you now. You might not have even listened when you were 21!”

A version of this story appeared in British GQ.

Fall means the start of the school year and holiday after holiday, which means busy mornings and even busier days (and chillier too!). If you feel like you never have the time to run to the grocery store and pick up tons of ingredients for endless weeknight dinners, we feel you. And with grocery prices still climbing, the last thing you want is a recipe that requires a long shopping list but still leaves you wanting more.

These 10 fall dinners check all the boxes. They're some of the easiest and quickest weeknight meals you can make, and best of all, each one requires no more than 10 ingredients, so you won't have to stock up on a bunch of extras.

The best weeknight dinners use pantry powerhouse ingredients to bring big flavor in a short time, and these creamy harissa chickpeas are a prime example. Harissa, tomato paste, and coconut milk join forces with chickpeas to create a saucy one-pan dinner that’s as quick to make as it is wildly craveable.

These cranberry brie turkey melts are precisely what they call for: rustic slices of artisan bread, tangy cranberry sauce, creamy buttery brie, and a mound of garlicky leftover turkey.

Not all sheet-pan dinners are created equal. Sheet-pan pork chops with apples falls into the camp of excellence, packing in flavor with a short-ingredient list onto one pan, all of which comes together in just over a half an hour.

Tossed in a fresh garlic-burst cherry tomato sauce and served with slabs of bubbling browned feta, these chickpeas are your weeknight ticket to protein-packed dinnertime bliss.

With the addition of one of fall’s flavor superstars—pumpkin, of course!—spaghetti carbonara gets a seasonal twist that'll have you craving it all season long. Adding pumpkin puree gives a creamy, silky, and subtly sweet boost to the otherwise simple sauce.

In this easy, hands-off version, we’re cooking thinly-sliced steak low and slow in a rich broth until it’s fall-apart delicious, and then throwing in the broccoli near the end so it cooks just long enough to become tender. After that, all you need is a pot of rice, and dinner is served!

Don't let chicken breasts have all the fun! Chicken thighs are super-flavorful, easy to cook, and SO delicious with sweet potatoes and apples. Try it for dinner any night this fall.

We’re big fans of one-pot pastas and French onion soup-flavored everything, so it was just a matter of time until we combined those two awesome things in one dish. Meet this one-pot French onion soup pasta, which is destined to become one of your favorite weeknight dinners.

Our creamy Tuscan chicken has consistently been one of our most-popular recipes since we published it, which has inspired our test kitchen to create countless iterations. Practically anything is delicious swimming in this creamy Tuscan-inspired sauce, but this vegetarian white bean dinner is our favorite.

This is a true 30-minute meal, and it calls for ingredients that you might already have on hand, saving you a trip to the grocery store. #6633. “It’s Always About Me and What I Need or What I Want to See Out in the World”: Rick Owens on Reuniting With Adidas

“Everything I do is completely selfish,” says Rick Owens about his new Adidas collaboration, which is the latest in his off-and-on relationship with the athleticwear mega-brand. “It’s always about me and what I need or what I want to see out in the world.”

Owens is beaming in from Claridge’s hotel in London, where he was delayed because he had trouble connecting to Wi-Fi. He’s there because his longtime partner Michèle Lamy is a guest judge on RuPaul’s Drag Race. When he does appear on my screen, his face is all sharp angles framed by his signature jet-black hair parted down the middle and hanging pin straight; his nails are painted (black, of course) and on his long, equine nose is perched a pair of oversized, architectural glasses.

Owens is much like you: he suddenly knows a lot of runners. In fact, many of them are part of his “family,” a phrase he lovingly uses to describe those who work with him or are fans of the brand he’s nurtured for the better part of three decades. “So when I see them suit up and put on a branded trainer that’s not ours, it just feels like, ‘oh, we’ve got a hole.’ I mean, this is the hole that we need to fill.”

So Owens is back at it with Adidas, this time leveraging their springblade technology, a series of futuristic blades at the sole of the shoe. Owens has applied them to a gaiter-like boot and runner, and they have a characteristic futuristic, avant-garde look. “Having the opportunity to use somebody else’s technology—when they’re the best at what they do—and to be able to make runners … and to be able to get my team out of their other branded fucking sneakers and into ours, that was my motivation,” Owens said with his usual candor. “And we’re able to do it in a way that everybody can engage.”

The shoes were first revealed back in June during Owens’s runway show for the spring 2027 collection, and their dramatic, Brutalist silhouette was the perfect complement to his lean, somewhat regal ready-to-wear designs. It borrowed from his existing “Taco” series, named so as it's essentially a folded piece of fabric over the foot, yielding a deflated bag shape. “The crumpled volume feels careless and opulent at the same time,” Owens said, before adding, “at the same time, I’m half-Mexican and love tacos.”

Indeed, the shoes were just a small part of the larger Adidas collaboration, which included ready-to-wear, like sweeping hooded capes, tracksuit pants in lean and oversized silhouettes, sharp-shouldered sleeveless tunics, and jackets and bodysuits that were inflated using internal fans. The result was a mix between those blow-up Halloween costumes and what happens to Violet Beauregarde when she turns into a blueberry in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. “I always think about how can I do a runway show that is impactful without being wasteful,” Owens said. “Without building sets that are going to be knocked down and thrown away. That’s wasteful.”

“The idea of using air and garments just fits into that,” he continued. “It’s something so pure and simple—and blending technology with something so naive, there was such charm in that. Inflated garments have been around for a long time. I mean, the Japanese workers have been using them for a long time, but then Adidas took it up, I don’t know, like 20 years ago or something. But then I found that in their archives, and so I thought, ‘Well, that’s timely.’”

And, yes, Rick-heads, those inflatable pieces will be produced for purchase. “I never wanted my runways to be an impossible dream,” he says. “In the old days, you would see runway shows with these women as these fantastic Thanksgiving Day parade floats, just these huge concoctions, and then the designer would come out at the end in jeans and a T-shirt. It deflated everything to me! It told me that the designer doesn’t believe in what he’s doing, and he’s not living it. It’s like saving your china for Sunday, or for special occasions. I want to be able to make stuff that people can have access to, and that is part of their everyday lives. So yeah, sure, there’s theater and exaggeration in what I do, but it’s connected to real life or my perception of it, which is more exaggerated than a lot of people, granted, but it’s for sale.”

While Owens is, let’s say, skeptical of the proliferation of collaborations—“If I see another collab, I’m going to roll my eyes until I fall over,” he said—the reason his with Adidas works is that they clearly give him the creative freedom to do as he pleases and it comes from a real place. It’s no big secret that Owens, with his lean physique and his at-home gym, is somewhat obsessed with working out. “When I changed my body in my 30s, when I took steroids, and started working out, it satisfied any kind of vanity the clothes would have been for. It was so much more profound than putting on an outfit. It was changing your entire bone structure. It was changing the foundation that the clothes were going to be on.”

Today his go-to gym outfit is pretty simple though—baggy shorts and thin T-shirts, and, when he’s traveling, he’ll often just wear hotel slippers. “I don’t really wear sneakers,” he says. “I’m just always in platforms.” Gym shoes, he says, take up too much room in his carry-on.

“So with Adidas, that’s my next step—to make a good workout gym shoe,” he said. “Super light and flat.”

Rick Owens for Adidas springblade shoes will range from $590 to $850 and will be available for purchase on November 17th at adidas.com, rickowens.eu, and select retailers.

#6632. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6627. Vogue Etiquette: Kelly Cutrone and Bozoma Saint John-Watson Have Very Different Ideas About How to Behave at Work

In 1948, Vogue published its 658-page Book of Etiquette, compiled by editor Millicent Fenwick, featuring how-tos, dos and don’ts, and the proper politesse for a remarkably varied set of scenarios. But as Fenwick writes in the introduction: “Etiquette is based on tradition, and yet it can change.” Some 75 years later, Oh, Behave! is a new monthly Vogue column in which experts sound off on today’s ever-evolving social etiquette.

There are two kinds of bosses: those who believe in work-life balance, and those who consider the very phrase a red flag. Kelly Cutrone, fashion’s legendary ball-breaker and founder of People’s Revolution, belongs firmly to the latter camp. Bozoma Saint John-Watson, a former marketing executive at Apple Music, Uber, and Netflix, is a little more forgiving. She’ll let you leave the office before your boss. She might even approve of wearing shorts to work.

For this installment of Oh, Behave!, we asked these two formidable women for a little workplace wisdom. Cutrone has lately been busy with everything from Farm to Fashion, a documentary about sheep and sustainable fashion, to Grindr’s Halloween festivities, while Saint John-Watson has brought her larger-than-life personality to The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills. From carrying a Birkin to an entry-level interview to answering late-night emails from your boss, we put the same workplace dilemmas to both women. Their answers are occasionally in agreement, frequently at odds, and never short on opinions. As for which woman you’d rather work for? We’ll leave that up to you.

Can you bring an iced coffee to a job interview?

Cutrone: No. Feeding and hydrating yourself before an interview is always a good idea. This isn’t a casual moment. No one wants a ring stain on their lacquer desk from your matcha bubble tea, or whatever the fuck you’re drinking. No.

Saint John-Watson: Yes, you can, but only if you bring one to your interviewer and you know whether or not they’d like coffee. You should email them and ask them. “I’m gonna get an iced coffee. Would you like one? If not, what else can I get you on my way in?”

Is arriving 20 minutes early for an interview punctual or presumptuous?

Cutrone: Presumptuous. People have a schedule for a reason. If you wanna arrive 20 minutes early and stand outside, that’s totally fine. Arrive early, but do it on the DL.

Saint John-Watson: That is presumptuous. You don’t know what they’ve got going on. Arrive five minutes ahead of time. Maybe 20 minutes outside the building, and then go up the elevator five minutes before.

Cutrone: Why would you want to embellish your résumé? It’s so easy to find out anything. I think it should be factual. Otherwise it’s fraud, and you’re applying for a job—you’re not there to scam people!

Saint John-Watson: You shouldn’t embellish at all, because in this day and age, it can be fact-checked pretty easily. But I do think using beautiful adjectives and great verbs will help to enhance the action that you took or the results that you had in your job. That’s probably as far as the embellishment should go.

Can you carry a Birkin to an interview for an entry-level position?

Cutrone: I wouldn’t. I think it’s a bit of a hyperflex. The first question is: ‘How did you get that Birkin?’ A Birkin is a signal, right? It’s like a stop sign. It reads to the average person like, “I’m rich, and I have good taste." But to people who actually have good taste, they would probably see that as in poor taste. Why do you have to scream it? I wouldn’t necessarily be impressed by that.

Saint John-Watson: It depends what the position is. If you are interviewing for a luxury job, then yes, carry the Birkin because maybe they want to see that you have taste, and maybe you should talk about how in the hell you acquired the Birkin on the salary you’re about to receive. But if you’re going in for a job outside the luxury space, keep the Birkin at home. Leave it there.

Is a post-interview thank-you email sufficient, or does a handwritten note still carry weight?

Cutrone: There’s nothing better than a handwritten note. I think there’s something super heartfelt and really chic about a handwritten note. I would do both. Some people don’t really check their emails, and some people don’t check their mailbox. Like, I check my mailbox every two weeks.

Saint John-Watson: I think in this day and age, an email is sufficient. A handwritten note depends on the industry. If you’re going for a job in tech, please don’t write a handwritten note. They won’t read it.

Cutrone: Being overfamiliar. Chewing gum. Wearing a ton of piercings—like, for me, it freaks me out. I personally don’t love it. Showing your midriff. Talking poorly about your last employer. Not making eye contact. Speaking in slang.

Saint John-Watson: Have questions at the end of the interview! And don’t read them off your phone! Commit them to memory so at least you appear to have been a part of the conversation. And don’t just talk about yourself, my God! Talk about the work, talk about them. Make it a conversation.

Can you leave the office before your boss does?

Cutrone: If I hear the phrase “work-life balance,” it's like a cue to me that this person is not going to make it. It does not exist in the PR or the fashion world. If that’s what you wanna do, you should be a receptionist at a dentist’s office. If somebody who works for me says, “Well, I have Pilates,” that’s not my problem. Why are you scheduling a Pilates class two weeks before fashion week at 6:30 p.m.? If your boss works late, it would be appropriate to say, “Would you like me to stay late and help you take some of this work off your plate?” How about that? What a sweet idea.

Saint John-Watson: Yes. You can leave the office before your boss does, but only if it is clearly understood the time you’re expected to be in and out.

Is it acceptable to eat lunch at your desk? What about particularly smelly foods?

Cutrone: Definitely not a good idea. I don’t like to sit next to people who are eating on planes or in my office or anything like that. I don’t wanna smell your cheese, and I don’t like the smell of meat. No one wants to see you eat.

Saint John-Watson: You can eat your lunch at your desk if you’re working. But if you are kicking up your feet and relaxed, sipping on your juice and eating your very fragrant food, then you probably should take it outside or take it into the break room. There’s no need to eat your lunch at your desk if you’re not working.

Can you wear pimple patches to the office?

Cutrone: I mean, if you work at Allure. If you’re a biophysicist, maybe. Palo Alto, probably. If I had to make a general statement: No to the pimple patches. I’d say get a facial or get on some sort of program and take care of your skin.

Saint John-Watson: I think in this day and age, you can wear pimple patches to the office, but please don’t cover your entire face with them. You should probably go see your doctor if it’s really that bad.

Is crying at your desk acceptable, or should tears be reserved for the bathroom?

Cutrone: Get control of your emotions. If you wanna cry, I get it. Do everything that you can in your power to remove yourself from your coworkers and your work environment. I used to, at People’s Revolution, go in the stairwell to cry. It’s distracting to people, and it’s catchy. People catch vibes in offices.

Saint John-Watson: It depends on what you’re crying about. If the tears are about frustration, anger at your boss, or anything that could be misunderstood, then you probably wanna take it to the bathroom and call in one of your closest colleagues to come in there and talk you down. But if the tears are because everybody’s disappointed in the results of the work, I think it’s okay to show the passion.

If your boss asks you to pick up their dry cleaning, can you say it’s not in your job description?

Cutrone: Yes, you can. But when there are six other people there that are waiting to get up through that glass ceiling, you have to assume that when you don’t get the dry cleaning, your name’s not gonna be on your boss’s first pick list. Reciprocation.

Saint John-Watson: I think it’s okay to say that, but you probably want to find a diplomatic way to say it. I would ask if they needed help with other things in the office so that they could go pick up their own dry cleaning. Because clearly something else is going on in the office that’s keeping them from running their personal errands.

Are shorts ever appropriate office attire?

Cutrone: It depends on where you work, and it depends on the length of the shorts. Is it a Daisy Duke? If you work at Hooters, I guess yes. (I don’t even know if that’s still open.) If you’re a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader, yeah. It's great! If you work at an insurance company, that’s probably not the best look.

Saint John-Watson: Girl, I’ve worked in tech. I’ve seen every kind of workplace attire. Shorts are fine. Just don’t let them be booty shorts. We don’t need to see your cheeks in the office.

How much personal flair should you bring to your office wardrobe?

Cutrone: Work is not a place for you to express yourself. It’s a place for you to express the genetics of the brand or the company that you’re working at. Could you imagine if you went into Louis Vuitton and someone was eating, like, a bowl of Cheerios with big ear gauges in, and was like, “Hey, how y’all doing today?”

Saint John-Watson: I once had a well-meaning senior executive tell me not to wear red lipstick or red nail polish to the office because it would signal the wrong thing. I think you should go ahead and do it. Express yourself and make sure that you are also expressing your own personal brand in how you appear. I think that diversity in the workplace is a beautiful thing.

How soon after starting a new job can you go on vacation?

Saint John-Watson: If you work in fashion, you don’t get a vacation between January and March, and you don’t get a vacation from July 15 to October 15. You just don’t. I would say, “I’m so excited to have this job. I’m not in a hurry to go on vacation, but when would be the best time for you for me to plan my vacation?” How’s that for an idea?

Saint John-Watson: If you start the job in Q1, you should probably wait until the summer to take a vacation. If you start the job in October, I think you could take off for Christmas and New Year, or the holiday season and New Year, if the office is closed.

Can you use the office printer for personal matters, like printing return labels?

Cutrone: No. Buy a printer with your first paycheck. They cost $149. They’re available at Staples.

Saint John-Watson: Absolutely not. Do not use the company printer to print personal things, please. What if you print the wrong thing? Now you’ve got all kinds of personal information out. What if somebody picks it up, you know, mistakenly?

Is it tacky to post about every promotion and professional accomplishment on LinkedIn?

Cutrone: If you’re promoted from an assistant to a junior editor, or from an editor to a director, yes. If you get the bathroom pass for an extra 10 minutes, no.

Saint John-Watson: Girl, no. I love that. Go ahead and post every single promotion. I’ve always said that nobody celebrated me until I started celebrating myself. So let the people know you’re doing a great job.

What are your biggest office etiquette no-nos?

Cutrone: Your coworkers aren’t your friends! Do not go out drinking with your coworkers! Pretend your coworkers are your in-laws. Better to say less and do more.

Saint John-Watson: Especially in open-concept offices, don’t be too loud! Don't be a disruption to other people around you. Don’t play your music too loud. Don't even talk too loud. If you’re taking personal phone calls, take them outside. Just don’t be a distraction to other people.

Does an 11 p.m. email from your boss warrant an 11 p.m. response?

Cutrone: Technically, no. But most bosses have more than one employee. That boss is gonna remember who responded. If I send an email at 11 o’clock at night, I’m smart enough now to say “for tomorrow,” so my employees don’t have an issue with me from a labor perspective. But I do notice the ones who answer and are like, “Okay, cool, on it, handled,” versus somebody who responds the next morning. The proof is in the pudding. If you’re on a boat in the middle of nowhere, and you have to survive, who are you gonna pick? And that’s what a business is. It’s survival. It’s not a joke.

Saint John-Watson: If your boss is asking you about numbers for a deck they need to present in the morning, you should absolutely respond. If your boss is asking you about something that is due a week from now, then you can wait till the morning.

Is a thumbs-up emoji an acceptable response to an email from your boss?

Cutrone: My employee sent me the salute one. I didn’t even know what that was at the beginning. I had to search it in my ChatGPT, like, “What does this mean?” Once I figured it out, I thought to myself, even better than a thumbs-up. I like it because they know I’m running a military organization!

Saint John-Watson: Yes, but I would be very careful about the emojis. We know the meanings of different emojis. Please no eggplant emoji. But a heart or a smile, sure. Why not? It’s cute.

Is “per my last email” acceptable or passive-aggressive?

Cutrone: “Per my last email” from somebody who has a lower title than me is not acceptable. I personally, as a boss, prefer, like, “Hey, not sure if you saw this,” or “I’m bumping this up.” But “per my last email” is like, yeah, you’re not following through in the way that you should. I don’t like that vibe.

Saint John-Watson: No, that is aggressive. It’s not even passive. Remove the passive. It is aggressive.

Is using ChatGPT to write your emails efficient or just lazy?

Cutrone: I’ve had people with master's degrees in journalism from NYU and Columbia who use ChatGPT. I find it offensive. Like, I didn’t hire you to do that. I hired you because you have a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia. Why don’t you use it? Make your parents proud.

Saint John-Watson: At this point, it’s efficient. But you should know the context of the email. You don’t want to respond with ChatGPT, and you’re talking about something that was not in the prior email or not answering the right thing. ChatGPT is not the answer to everything.

Is it acceptable to turn your camera off during a Zoom meeting?

Cutrone: It depends on your title and where you are. If you’re an assistant, some people prefer that. You’re there to take notes, and I think that’s very appropriate and very respectful. That’s something I would ask your boss.

Saint John-Watson: Absolutely not. Please turn your camera on. There are so many ways to communicate. It’s not just voice. It’s also expression, and it’s a great way to connect with people. Just make sure you’re communicating the right thing with your face.

Is it acceptable to eat lunch during a Zoom meeting?

Cutrone: Absolutely not. It’s your job to feed yourself. I can’t stand when I’m producing an event with my team, and it’s like 6 p.m. and they go, “We’re hungry.” That’s not my problem. You should have eaten before you came here. Like, feed yourself. I mean, how much food do you actually need? You have a Zoom call at 2 p.m., eat at 1 p.m.. Nobody wants to watch you eat your food. It’s disgusting. So gross.

Saint John-Watson: No, we don’t wanna see you chewing. Nobody wants to see you chewing on the Zoom, so please don’t do that. You can wait till after the Zoom to eat, or hurry up and eat and then get on the Zoom.

What are your biggest email and Zoom etiquette no-nos?

Cutrone: Check your background. Blur it out or go on Amazon and get yourself a green screen, because nobody wants to see your Grateful Dead tour T-shirt in your closet. Look chic.

Saint John-Watson: Don’t CC everybody on every single email. Only CC the people who are supposed to know, but are not responsible for responding. Don’t just put people in there randomly.

#6625. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.
