#6594. Few Bags Have Had the Staying Power of Balenciaga’s Le City—Now It’s Turning 25

It’s hard to believe that 25 years have passed since Balenciaga’s Le City bag arrived on the scene—the design riffing on a motorcycle jacket, the sans-logo attitude unapologetically cool. A quarter-century is long enough that some see the bag mostly with nostalgia while others are discovering its It-status for the first time.

Certainly, in the midst of the mythic maison’s creative director shakeup—the departure of Pierpaolo Piccioli, the appointment of Martine Rose—Le City remains an enduring constant, riding out every era from its creation by Nicolas Ghesquière through Alexander Wang and Demna, who proposed his own version, the Neo City, in 2020.

Starting tomorrow, Balenciaga is kicking off Le City’s anniversary with celebratory activations in several cities around the world. Le City House will bow in its Paris hometown for nine days, with New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, Beijing, and Seoul staggered through the end of the year. The spaces also exist to launch a major collaboration involving the artist provocateur Damien Hirst. Folks, get ready for DAMIENCIAGA, a limited edition Le City capsule that transposes some of his famous works to the characteristic Arena leather.

A few days prior to the reveal, I made a site visit to the historic address of 10, Avenue George V, where Cristobal established his atelier and where customers more recently could purchase Demna’s Couture. Le City House is altogether different: a multi-modal, Y2K-coded experience that is sleek yet visitor-friendly and daresay playful.

Upon entering, a prototype of Le City from 2001—compact and in brown cotton canvas—sits in a see-through cube atop a Parisian bench painted glossy blue. There’s a floor-to-ceiling display of Le City as eye candy: bags in vivid shades of Maldives Green and Ultra Violet; in surface treatments such as tweed panels and brogue trims; and in novelty one-offs (including Ghesquière’s Multicolor City Mondriaan in red, yellow, and blue). Nearby are the “closets” that boast bags belonging to celebrity collectors such as Nicole Ritchie, the French footballer Hugo Ekitike, Clémence Poésy and Isabelle Huppert (each Le City House will feature different boldface names) propped with daily items and old Blackberry devices that double as labels (Ritchie’s, for instance, is from 2005). Small screens flash Parisian landmarks while a full-length panel rotates editorial, street style, and paparazzi photos. For all the glimpses of Kate Moss, Chloe Sevigny, Mary-Kate Olsen, and Sienna Miller, Le City is clearly the star.

Further back, past a metal railing bedecked with padlocks is the room with Hirst’s creations. The most rarefied, done by hand, is doused in splashes of pigment like his Spin Paintings and exists as an edition of 25. The others—his multicolored spots arranged like a butterfly; his mandala of wings; his uniform grid of dots; and a compilation of his ideas as embroidered patches—will be more widely available.

The second space, dubbed “Le Salon,” functions like a leather workshop-turned-bag spa. Artisans stationed on Platner stools will be personalizing bags: replacing the lacing along the top handle, offering custom charms, and hand-painting or etching initials on the rectangular pocket mirror that has remained one of Le City’s defining details. People can also make an appointment to have their old bags assessed for extra refresh services.

Finally, there is a photo kiosk programmed as though straight out of a teen magazine quiz circa the 1990s, only that the theme is not crushes or careers, but which Le City is right for you. One result might yield Le City Moto (“Bold, confident and a little rebellious”); another Le City Mini Backpack (“Your match understands that you have your hands full”). Alas, you do not actually receive a free bag.

If Le City House represents a fun, public-facing commemoration of Balenciaga’s best-selling bag, the maison’s vast archive on the outskirts of Paris offers the contextual perspective. This is where, thanks to a tour provided by Heritage and Cultural Director, Gaspard de Massé, I found myself learning about how the Le City—eschewing conspicuous branding but rather adorned with a sexy mix of laces, buckles, and studs—almost never came to be.

Nicolas Ghesquière with the Balenciaga city bag in 2004. Photographed by Robert Fairer, Vogue, September 2004

As the lore goes and he recounts, Ghesquière was working on a motorcycle-inspired bag in 2000 when Moss saw a version and showed interest in it. He gave her one and offered others to his inner circle—women like Marie-Amélie Sauvé, Carine Roitfeld, and Emmanuelle Alt—initially calling it Le Lariat, then Le Motorcycle. Le First and Le City followed based on their sizes, until eventually, the latter stuck for the entire family.

The 3,000-square-meter temperature- and humidity-controlled space is filled not only with the kind of heaving mobile shelving units found in institutional archives, but also the storage of patrimonial furniture, Cristobal’s actual library, and two stunning paintings positioned upright (one is by Bernard Buffet of his wife, Annabel, wearing a pink Balenciaga gown; the other, surprisingly, is of Gabrielle Chanel in a soigné white ensemble by A.M. Cassandre).

Of course, we end up over at the units stacked with Le City models, never carried and originating from the workshops. You need not be prone to It-bag lust to marvel over the sheer number and variety—some 879 at last count. Dream of a shade and it’s probably in the mix. There are evolutions and iterations: the burnished studs that morphed to resemble thimbles; the brogue trims that evoked Derby shoes; the metal hardware; the Part Time with its seam down the middle or the square Velo format (presumably to fit inside a bicycle basket).

So how, in De Massé’s mind, has Le City remained such a hero piece? “I think it’s extremely identifiable, and because of that, it doesn’t really feel like taking a risk,” he says. “You know that you’re buying this particular bag for a specific reason; and undoubtedly, part of that reason is that you’re joining all those other people who already own one. There’s something of a community spirit around it; it’s not an exclusively ultra-luxury community, nor is it mass market. It occupies this interesting space somewhere in between.”

He goes on: “For today’s generations, it can also function as a kind of madeleine de Proust, something that evokes a particular moment or memory. I remember Britney Spears in the 2000s, for example. Even if I didn’t personally experience that period in the same way, those images are part of my imagination, and the bag allows me to reconnect with an aesthetic or a moment that I liked. There’s something reassuring about that. Of course, it’s different for everyone; but I think that recognizability, combined with the fact that the bag feels approachable and accessible, is fundamental to its success.”

Indeed, few bags have had such staying power independent of the promotion machine, off-duty model shot, or hype cycle. But Le City is a bag that also happens to wear well. The non-boxy shape proved easy to carry and the Arena leather already appeared lived-in, becoming more cherished as it was subjected to life’s vicissitudes. Remember Mary-Kate’s endless attachment to her mint green bag—not despite, but possibly because of, its glaring red wine stain?

Although Le City has never needed reinvention, it was updated in 2024 when various vintage styles were studied together, so that the new construction—hand-assembled from 25 panels—signified a faithful “amalgamation.” The launch was announced with a campaign of portraits by Mario Sorrenti starring Moss as well as Mona Tougaard, Juyeon, and Yang Chaoyue. Last year, an “ultra-luxe” version marked the first runway appearance of Le City, coinciding with Piccioli’s debut. Another campaign followed, this time by David Sims—Le City’s original fashion photographer—marking a reunion and full-circle moment.

The campaign for the Hirst series features Ritchie dressed in a draped yellow top over jeans, her gaze smoldering as the mandala butterfly bag hangs from her forearm. Ekitike cradles one of the patchwork styles alongside the Seine.

For Hirst, Le City was imprinted on his mind even before the collaboration opportunity arose. “I think everyone knows it, don’t they? It’s one of the most iconic bags of the last 25 years,” he tells Vogue via email. “You associate it with the noughties, with Kate Moss, yet it’s still remained so relevant.”

This is a whole other Hirst than when he was preserving sharks in tanks or encrusting skulls with diamonds, yet the bags are not without a hint of subversion seeing as the original Spot Paintings were named after pharmaceutical drugs or chemical compounds and the Butterfly mandalas alluded to mortality, spirituality, and the passage of time.

Hugo Ekitike with the Balenciaga “DAMIENCIAGA” bag.

It’s likely his 25 hand-painted Le Cities (or is it Les Citys?) will have collector value. They look like they were a thrill to make, the layers of vivid paint leaving barely a trace of original surface. The artist suggests the best part will be when people make the bags their own. “It’s not just a ‘Balenciaga’ or a ‘Hirst’… they’re adding their personality to it. And I think that’s what fashion is all about.”

They are also a reminder that fashion loves a revival. Each Le City House will be reintroducing people to a cultural moment well before quiet luxury, and whatever we are shifting into now. Thanks to the anniversary, the bag is definitely back; the bolder, the better. To wit, Le City x Hirst even boasts a logo of sorts: ‘Damienciaga’ appears in a fine silver script along one side.

#6593. Peppermint Bark Cookie Bars

Line a 13×9-inch pan with parchment paper, letting the ends extend up the sides. In a large bowl, use a hand mixer or stand mixer to cream the butter, sugar and vanilla extract until it’s light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg yolks until they’re combined.

In another bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour and salt. Gradually beat the flour mixture into the creamed mixture just until no streaks of flour remain.

In the top of a double boiler or a metal bowl over hot water, melt the dark chocolate, stirring until it’s completely smooth. Remove the bowl from the heat and spread the dark chocolate over the cooled bars.

Editor’s Tip: Never let the water touch the bottom of the bowl, or it will burn the chocolate. Also, try not to get any water into the chocolate, or it will seize.

Repeat the melting and spreading process with the white chocolate, then immediately sprinkle the top with crushed peppermint candies while the chocolate is still wet.

#6592. 31 Thanksgiving Desserts to Cap Your Holiday Feast

There’s Thanksgiving dinner, and then there are Thanksgiving desserts. These are two separate events, and in between, it’s perfectly fine to take a disco nap. (In fact, we recommend it.)

“This is the magnum opus of Thanksgiving dessert recipes,” writes one reader whose 90-year-old grandfather asked for a repeat performance. “You bet your boots I will—it’s the best apple pie, ever.”

A colossal, self-serve mousse is a baller host move—no tidy slicing, no fussy garnishing, no jockeying for oven space. Set out bowls and spoons and let guests help themselves. Vanilla lovers, try our Colossal Crème Brûlée.

Butter-toasted pecans get the glory, but sour cream does the work, balancing both the gooey pecan layer and the pile of whipped cream. Between them? A thick layer of silky brown sugar custard.

A slice of Thanksgiving pie is nice, but how about a slice of pumpkin flan under a veneer of caramel? This one takes a page from Puerto Rican flan de queso, with cream cheese lending richness, tang, and luxurious texture.

Consider this pie a tangy exclamation point to the holiday meal: cranberry-lime curd in a flaky cream cheese crust, crowned with billows of meringue.

Brown sugar takes some of the fuss out of caramel cake’s famously finicky frosting while browned butter adds toasty depth. Spread it over tender yellow cake layers and finish with flaky salt.

Silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice: This is pumpkin pie done right. Sweetened condensed milk gives the custard its richness; maple syrup and vanilla round out the flavor.

Skip the rolling pin: Buttered phyllo encloses an orange-scented custard, with crumpled sheets forming a dramatically ruffled top. Cinnamon sugar adds crunch to this no-roll pie.

This plush pumpkin spice cake wears a thick swoop of tangy cream cheese frosting. Bake the cake a day ahead, then add the frosting in the lull between dinner and dessert.

If most holiday desserts feel a tad too sweet for you, herbal rosemary and fruity olive oil give this cake just enough savory elements to justify a second helping.

Blanketing quartered apples with rough-puff pastry feels rustic enough, but once baked and inverted, this shimmering, blushing tart dominates the holiday table.

Sweet potato, warming spices, and orange zest get a gloss of dark chocolate in this autumnal loaf cake. Bake it up to three days ahead, leaving the ganache for later.

A deeply browned top and cracked sides are the goal here, not a baking mishap. Underneath: a custardy, pumpkin-spiced cheesecake that needs neither a crust nor a water bath.

Pecan pie meets Hawaiian-style butter mochi in this chewy, coconut-milk-rich cake. Miso-and-maple-coated pecans bring salty-sweet crunch, with some sinking into the batter as the cake bakes.

This date cake blanketed in toffee sauce tastes like cozying up by the fireside after a game of football on the lawn. Bake the unsauced cake a day ahead, then rewarm before finishing.

Cinnamon-spiced pumpkin cake rolled around walnut-studded cream cheese filling needs little embellishment. A dusting of powdered sugar is plenty—each slice supplies its own dramatic swirl.

This glamorous layer cake, with jewel-toned swipes of cranberry jam, white chocolate–cream cheese frosting, and sugared cranberries, looks and tastes like winter is coming (in the best possible way).

A no-bake Oreo crust, a rich chocolate filling, and a tower of whipped cream come together in this shut-the-room-up dessert.

Caramel-glazed apple halves crown this nutty upside-down cake, all baked in the same skillet used to brown the fruit. A scoop of vanilla ice cream on top? We wouldn’t say no.

A floral, earthy saffron soak gives this sponge cake a pudding-like texture and its vibrant yellow color, while pistachios add nutty crunch.

Cranberries with dinner and again for dessert? Absolutely. Tart filling hides between layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust in this Linzer tart. Prefer individual portions? Try these cranberry hand pies.

Pumpkin crumb cake is like the brownie of Thanksgiving desserts: easy to tote and slice for sharing. Here, sweet rice flour gives the cake a chewy bounce beneath a buttery, crispy-crumbly pecan streusel.

The ultraflaky crust barely contains the lofty, fudgy almond filling, but have faith: It will puff and dome as it bakes, then settle back into sliceable form once cool.

Alternate layers of pumpkin and chocolate batter create this Bundt cake’s mesmerizing marbling—no knife-swirling necessary. A blanket of chocolate ganache makes it equally appealing to the pumpkin crowd and the chocolate diehards.

Whole roasted birds, spatchcocked showstoppers, braised legs, breasts for smaller gatherings, and more ways to put turkey at the center of the table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

#6591. These Panera Snowman Cups Are Only Available for a Day—Here’s How to Get One

The Panera Snowman Cup is giving the Starbucks Bearista Cup some cozy competition. Here's what you need to know about the limited-edition mystery boxes.

I don’t generally need an incentive to stop at Panera in December. Any of those delicious soups in a bread bowl is a fairly convincing argument on its own. But this year, the chain is giving us another reason to visit: collectible glass snowman cups, with a chance to get one free.

If you’ve been admiring the Starbucks Bearista cup, these little snowmen might also deserve a spot on your wish list. Panera’s version comes in a mystery box containing one of two designs, naughty or nice. The free cup offer runs on Dec. 3, and with only 12 available at each participating cafe, there are a few details to keep in mind before you go.

The limited-edition glass cups come in two designs inspired by the naughty-and-nice theme of Panera’s holiday packaging. Each mystery box holds one snowman cup, so you won’t know which you’ve received until you open it.

There are also a few new things to drink while you admire your cute cup. Panera’s new holiday menu, rolling out this week, includes peppermint white mocha and pistachio white mocha beverages. Both flavors are available as a latte, iced coffee or Frozen Java, finished with peppermint bark pieces or pistachio pieces. The iced coffees have sweet cream cold foam, and the lattes and Frozen Java drinks get whipped cream.

On Dec. 3, the first 12 customers at each participating U.S. cafe who make a qualifying purchase of $25 or more will receive a free Snowman Cup, while supplies last. There’s a limit of one per person, so you may want to make that Panera outing a breakfast date.

You’ll need to order inside the cafe at the cashier. Kiosk, Rapid Pick-Up, drive-thru, catering and delivery orders—including those placed through third-party sites—don’t qualify.

If you don’t get your hands on one of those first 12 boxes, you’ll have another way to find a snowman. A limited number of cups will also be available through the Panera Shop for $22 each. An online sale date hasn’t been announced yet, so keep an eye on the shop if you’re hoping to grab one.

Are you going to be first in line at Panera on Dec. 3? Let us know in the comments below!

#6590. 9 Best Eyeliners for Older Women That Glide on With Ease

When I shop for eyeliner these days, I feel like I’m going into a restaurant with a list of dietary restrictions. I have always had hooded eyes, but at 46, the hooding is more pronounced. I have sensitive eyes, too, and fine lines starting to set in. In short, I’m looking for an eyeliner to play up my gaze while downplaying any discomfort or signs of aging. It’s a balancing act, to be sure, but it’s one that the best eyeliners for older women can accomplish with finesse—and if it becomes tempting to skip eyeliner altogether, consider this advice from a pro: “Eyeliner actually becomes more important as we age,” says makeup artist Stevi Christine. “Lashes tend to thin over time, and a liner at the roots helps bring back that youthful fullness.”

Since I’ve found a few formulas that I swear by—including the Laura Mercier pencil that’s on this list—I see what Christine means. On days when I do wear eyeliner, I look more awake, chipper, and polished than on days when I don’t. The trick? Finding formulas that are not only flattering, but gentle on the eyes. Formulas for older women should also be easy to apply and remove without tugging at the lids. Ahead, find the eyeliners that check every box.

What type of eyeliner is best for mature eyes?

“Because of its rich color payoff, a smooth gel or cream eyeliner pencil is a great choice for enhancing mature eyes,” says Wagener. “Eyeliner with a creamy texture glides on effortlessly, providing a defined line that won’t tug at delicate skin.” On the other hand, Wagener tells her mature clients to steer clear of most liquid felt-tip liners. “They can be less forgiving and very difficult to use,” she says.

What to Look for in an Eyeliner for Older Women

When it comes to choosing an eyeliner for women over 50, makeup artists keep a few key factors in mind.

How should you apply eyeliner to mature eyes?

“Depending on the eye shape, I often line only the outer third or outer half of the upper lash line and then tightline the whole length of the lash line from underneath,” says Patinkin. “This is a great technique for lots of reasons.” First, she says, it contributes to a lifted look at the outer corner of the eyes, where the shadow is thicker. The technique also helps define the shape of the eyes without “eating up lid space,” she says. Tightlining is another technique makeup artists favor for mature eyes. “It makes the lashes look thicker because you’re filling in gaps between the roots of the lashes,” Patinkin says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity makeup artists—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

#6589. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6588. The World's 50 Best Restaurants, According to ‘The 50’ Best List

Asador Etxebarri from the Spanish Basque Country won the title of world's best restaurant Wednesday night when The 50, the organization formerly known as 50 Best, announced its annual ranking during a ceremony in Lima, Peru. It was the first such event for The 50 in South America.

Situated between Bilbao and San Sebastián, Etxebarri claims some of the world's most famous chefs as major fans of Bittor Arginzoniz, who matches the characteristics of the wood in the grill with the plants and proteins sizzling over the flames. It was No. 2 on The 50 in 2025 and maintains one Michelin star. Tasting menus are around $337.

Wednesday was also a big night for Atomix in New York, which came in at No. 11 and was named Best Restaurant in North America. Junghyun Park took home the Chef's Choice Award.

A spot on The 50 is among the highest honors a restaurant can receive. (Disclosure: Bon Appétit editor in chief Jamila Robinson is a 50 Best Academy Chair.) The list favors some of the most expensive, elaborate cooking in the fine-dining world. It often rewards tasting menus that employ molecular gastronomy, but also celebrates the simple elegance of a Spanish grill, the sourcing mission of an Argentine steakhouse, or the laidback cool of Parisian neo-bistro.

This year’s ceremony ran into controversy earlier in the year when it was announced that it would be hosted in Abu Dhabi, which has faced criticism for human rights violations. In June, it was announced that the ceremony would instead be hosted in Peru, home to Maido, the Lima restaurant that won No. 1 last year. Maido is not eligible for this year’s list. After winning the top spot, it moves to the organization’s Best of the Best list alongside other past number ones like Barcelona’s Disfrutar and New York’s Eleven Madison Park.

Quintonil landed at No. 4. The two-Michelin starred restaurant in Mexico City led by Jorge Vallejo and Alejandra Flores, serves dishes that revolve around local, pre-Hispanic ingredients, which come together in energized and unexpected ways throughout its multi-course prix-fixe menu. A November menu listed on its website was priced around $327 per person for a meal that included lobster in a pipián verde with makrut lime, and an heirloom white corn tamal made with ayocote beans and young corn cream.

At Alchemist in Copenhagen (No. 3), chef Rasmus Munk oversees a meal that skews sci-fi with dishes that mimic brains and eyeballs and a show that advertises “up to 50 impressions,” both edible and “purely experiential.” It holds two Michelin stars and was ranked fifth on The 50 last year.

Gaggan in Bangkok (No. 2) claimed the title of Asia's Best Restaurant behind the creative, genre-bending Indian cooking of Gaggan Anand.

Critics of the World’s 50 Best have raised questions around its voting practices, which do not demand that voters pay for their own meals. The organization, for its part, explains that the list is voted on by more than 1,100 voters across 28 regions, a quarter of whom are new each year. The voting body is made up of equal parts chefs and restaurateurs, food writers, and “well-travelled gourmets,” as the The 50 website puts it. Aside from the Academy Chairs, voters must remain anonymous.

There is no set criteria for what makes a restaurant the best, and “every style of restaurant in the world is eligible,” though the list skews completely towards high-end dining even as other best-of links have begun to include street food venues, for instance.

Ana Ros, the chef at three Michelin-starred Hisa Franko in Slovenia, published a statement on Instagram last month explaining why she would not attend the ceremony in Lima. “Success within the ranking has come to depend increasingly on visibility within the system,” she wrote. “…When visibility becomes the currency, the ability to promote a restaurant in this system risks becoming as important as the work happening inside it.”

Ros, who won the award for best female chef from The 50 in 2017, told Bon Appétit that restaurants and tourism boards “more or less” know who the anonymous voters are, and they often have to make decisions about whether to pay for travel, meals, and other entertainment to try and boost their standing.

“With more rules and a little bit more control, this list can really shine again,” she said in an interview.

Hisa Franko was No. 60 on the ranking of 51-100 this year. It was 69th last year and No. 48 in 2024.

Ros said seeing her restaurant at any place on the list was “a fantastic result” and she would be wishing everyone all the best at the ceremony.

#6586. Around the World in 80 Handbags—Inside a New Istanbul Exhibition Devoted to the Exceptional Accessory

A handbag is rarely just a handbag. It can be a keeper of secrets, a declaration of status, or a traveling companion—not to mention a rather expensive place to keep one’s keys. At Beymen Tersane, Istanbul’s newest shopping destination, it takes on another role: that of a vessel for cultural memory. This idea lies at the heart of “Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” an exhibition inaugurated to mark the cultural complex’s opening, bringing together 80 creations from 55 international brands in a dialogue between contemporary design and the layered heritage of Anatolia and the Ottoman Empire.

Curated by Laurence Benaïm, the presentation is less an exercise in historical illustration than an invitation to look at memory through a different perspective. The challenge, she explained, was not to reproduce traditional motifs or reduce Ottoman references to decorative shorthand, but to translate their spirit into a modern design language. Her vision was that of a “curiosity cabinet of dreams and craftsmanship,” where newly commissioned pieces sit alongside archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

The journey unfolds across seven chapters, each exploring a different facet of the relationship between bags and cultural memory. Precious Envelopes includes the pouches once used by ambassadors to carry letters, imperial decrees and secrets, a reminder that the art of keeping things under wraps has a long history. Heavenly Gardens draws on the flora and fauna of İznik ceramics and Ottoman palace gardens, while Golden Jewels explores the allure of gold. Magical Boxes considers the bag as guardian of private possessions and hidden treasures, a function that has hardly lost its appeal. Nomad Memories traces the weaving, leatherwork, and saddlebag traditions that traveled from Central Asia to Anatolia. A final glance towards the future brings in three designs by young Turkish talents, selected through a competition supported by Beymen in collaboration with local universities. Among the historical highlights is a piece of luxurious archaeology: a massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

A massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

For Benaïm, the point is that heritage should not be treated as a fixed inheritance or an exercise in nostalgia. “Heritage isn’t about looking backwards. It’s about carrying the beauty of the past into the future,” she remarked. The exhibition, more than two years in the making, is a “love letter to Turkish culture” and an exploration of the ways in which fashion can preserve cultural memory while giving it new meaning. “There is no luxury without soul, without heart and without love, and without a sense of time,” Benaïm added.

The choice of venue is not incidental. Beymen Tersane occupies part of the historic shipyard on the Golden Horn, a site stretching back some 600 years, reimagined by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA as a 12,000-square-meter destination for fashion, art, and lifestyle. Rather than imposing another conventional department-store interior on the monumental structure, the architects conceived a horizontal sequence of eight galleries.

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” features bags by 55 international brands including newly commissioned pieces and archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

For Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçı, the project continues the conversation started in 2023 with “Golden Opulence,” a 50th anniversary exhibition in which 50 international brands were commissioned for a unique piece. This time, the bag became the focus, “an object whose changing form and function offers a revealing record of shifting lifestyles, tastes and social codes,” Çapçı noted.

Rachid Mohamed Rachid, CEO of Mayhoola and chairman of Beymen, sees Beymen Tersane as part of a broader ambition to bring the cultural complexities of Turkey to the attention of the international luxury world. But there is something deeper at stake here than a showcase of commercial partnerships. “As Istanbul has always understood, the most interesting exchanges happen when different worlds meet without either having to surrender its identity,” he said.

And perhaps this is the point: The handbag, after all, is a meeting place of its own, a repository of craftsmanship, memory, and imagination. There is clearly more to it than what fits inside. Though isn’t it nice that it also accommodates a phone, a lipstick and a pair of sunglasses?

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag” is on view at Istanbul’s Beymen Tersane through February 8, 2027.

#6585. The 15 Best Appetizers at Trader Joe’s

Why is Trader Joe’s so good at making small foods? I’m thinking it’s Newton’s Third Law, providing balance to all of Costco’s extra-large foods. Remind me to bring this up at my next dinner party when I pull a batch of Parmesan Pastry Pups out of the air fryer to serve to my guests. If you’ve been a long-time shopper at Trader Joe’s, you know that this grocery store does frozen appetizers better than actual dinners. So if you’re preparing for marathon holiday hosting, here’s my list of the best bite-size apps, in order from the least messy to most messy. They can almost all be prepared in the air fryer too, which frees up your larger oven for the enchiladas I hope are for dinner. Always hoping.

Adorable little tarts! These are what I like to snatch at a wedding cocktail reception the second the servers glide through the saloon doors. Savory mushrooms, buttery pie crust. For a faux-made flourish, buy a package of chives to slice and sprinkle over.

Mess-o-meter: 1/10. You can pop the whole tartelette in your mouth and forget it ever even happened.

Love this new addition. You can fry them up before guests arrive because they’re very very hot right out of the pan and the rice paper wrappers stay nicely crisp. My only gripe is these don’t come with a dipping sauce, so pick up a bag of scallions to slice and scatter over—nice touch—and the Gyoza Dipping Sauce. Or make your own with soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sugar.

Mess-o-meter: 1/10. These are also a one-to-two-bite chopstick situation with a well-contained filling.

An absolute icon in the Trader Joe’s frozen aisle. These fried mac and cheese balls are arancini’s Gen Z cousin, replacing its job at a quarter of the price (the price of cooking prep time, in this case). Adorable, delicious, crunchy, oozy. If these are at your party, served with a pepper jelly or spicy mayo getup, I won’t sneak out the backdoor like I usually do.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. You’ll need a cocktail napkin or little plate to help contain the ooze. Dip in marinara (fun) and it escalates to a 3.

You really want crab rangoons, but your guests will still be thrilled with this riff, which has a wee bit of jalapeño, not enough to shoot steam from your ear canals. Make sure to pick up a dipping sauce—Pepper Jelly, always, or Sweet Chili Sauce. Sometimes these can come out a little dry on the exterior, especially if you air-fry them. Try tossing (or spraying) them in oil for a crispier, browner exterior.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. Someone will probably drip dipping sauce on the tablecloth.

Another classic party food. These two-bite samosas have approx one Lego cube of potato, a single pea, and maybe a flake of cilantro inside, but they’re the perfect beer snack. For dunking, the Sri Lankan Mango Chutney would be nice here.

Mess-o-meter: 2/10. While the crust is nice and crisp, it stays pretty contained when you bite in.

Trader Joe’s dips are hit or miss—this one’s a hit. Not exactly queso like my mama made, but after a few tequilas no one seems to care. It’s thick molten cheese with a gentle kick. The key is to transfer it to a cute bowl, microwave it, and hide the original packaging deep in the recycling. I like Trader Joe’s Restaurant Style Tortilla Chips, which are sturdy and very salty, but others prefer the classic rounds or the moody blue corn ones. Your choice.

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. Impatient dippers will leave a trail of queso, these are facts of life.

Make a version of one of Bon Appétit’s swankiest yet simplest party tricks—marinated salami and almonds—with Trader Joe’s standbys. The rosemary-flavored Marcona almonds are buttery and crunchy. I don’t love the salami at Trader Joe’s, but the secret to this “recipe” is that the oil, lemon, and pepper make even the cheap stuff taste gourmet.

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. Oily! You’ll need a napkin or hunks of baguette to catch those drips.

I’ve been eating these French-accented ham pizzas (tartes, sure) as long as I’ve been shopping at Trader Joe’s, which is…20 years now. The crust is paper thin, the Gruyère is generously laden, and it cooks in under 15 minutes. If you’re sharing with guests, cut it into small rectangles to avoid floppy slices. (Or save the floppies for yourself.)

Mess-o-meter: 3/10. The toppings can be gooey and may overfloweth.

No cooking, just light assembly. Trader Joe’s recently added mortadella is great for draping directly into the mouth, but for an entertaining scenario, you can make these “mortadella moments” which are classy sliders. Trader Joe’s focaccia, sliced and toasted, will do the trick, or their ciabatta, sliced into small squares.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. Bread crumbs happen. Perhaps a pickle makes a run for it.

These baby shrimp bao need to be eaten pretty soon after steaming (or microwaving), so they’re great for, like, a Gilded Age viewing party where your guests are glued to the couch, waiting for you to bring them fresh snacks like the good servant you are. The buns are soft and spongy, the shrimp patties decently seasoned, and they’re easy to improve with carrots, cukes, and scallions. Plus, unlike a lot of TJ apps, they come with a lip-smacky lemongrass dipping sauce.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. These are pretty tidy but your added garnishes may fling about.

Keep it simple. Sometimes the best appetizer isn’t an air-fried novelty, but a nice cheese you’ve let come to room temperature—30 minutes, please—a salty cracker, and a pinch pot o’ jelly. Old Amsterdam is always in stores and the ultimate crowdpleaser, but go for goat cheese or blue cheese or even feta if you’re feeling festive. I’ve got other favorite Trader Joe’s cheeses here.

Mess-o-meter: 4/10. Expect typical cheese board detritus, like the tragic hollowed-out cheese rind.

Hello, these are mini Bloomin’ Onions! There are only two “flowers” to a box, so these are an appetizer for a more intimate occasion, unless you’re feeling ambitious and spendy. Invite me if you are. Make sure to cook until nicely golden brown and to pick up a bottle of Buttermilk Ranch (near the bagged salads) to accompany.

Mess-o-meter: 8/10. You will tear into these with your rabid paws, so fried onion petals will leave crumbs and oop, ya need to wipe your face a little there.

These are fried, tangled veggie tempura fritters that guests can pop into their mouths while leaving greasy fingerprints on your furniture. The soy dipping sauce could use a few fresh scallions or chives, but you can do that. These have been at Trader Joe’s for decades; they’re a classic for a reason.

Mess-o-meter: 8/10. It’s a fritter with crispy bits and pieces, but that’s why we love ’em.

Welcome to the flaky pastry portion of our evening. You might know these pups as “pigs in a blanket” but Joe has never been one to follow convention. (Just profits lol.) Pair with Hot Honey Mustard and always buy one more box than you think is needed.

Mess-o-meter: 9/10. Think of puff pastry’s flaky confetti as spontaneous party decor. It means your guests are having a good time, all over your rug.

For a homemade-ish appetizer, I like to do these easy puff pastry cheese twists from Dessert Person Claire Saffitz. The twists look nice but when you don’t have time for arts and crafts, I have a shortcut: Defrost puff pastry. Roll it out a smidge. Brush with egg wash. Sprinkle with cheese and spices. Bake at 400° until browned. Cut into squares. Bask in the glory.

Mess-o-meter: 10/10. This is a beautiful mess. But don’t worry about it. You’ll vacuum tomorrow.

#6584. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6583. Ocean Spray Just Gave Canned Cranberry Sauce A Chocolate Makeover

Someone finally saw the potential in those jiggly, ridged slices.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Canned cranberry sauce has some pretty stiff competition at Thanksgiving. Between the mashed potatoes, stuffing, and mac and cheese, that jiggly little side dish often gets treated like the ugly stepsister of the dinner table. And it probably doesn't help that it comes out looking exactly like the can it was packaged in.

But perhaps a little chocolate could improve its reputation.

Ocean Spray and Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés have teamed up with recipe developer Carolina Gelen on a new treat called Chocolate Covered Cranberry Sauce, taking the familiar Ocean Spray stuff and turning it into chocolate-coated discs, sold in packs of four.

If that sounds vaguely familiar, you may have seen Gelen's original Instagram video from 2023, when she experimented with dipping slices of canned cranberry sauce in chocolate (the recipe has since racked up more than 10 million views).

Ocean Spray's Kelvin Vuong said Gelen's recipe was exactly the kind of unexpected use for cranberry sauce the company wanted to share with more people. The brand eventually partnered with her and Compartés to turn the homemade recipe into something people could purchase—and Gelen is pretty thrilled to see her original experiment come this far.

"Getting to work with Ocean Spray and Compartés to turn that idea into something people across the country can try is incredibly exciting," she said in the announcement.

As for why this combination works, Compartés' creative director and chief chocolatier, Jonathan Grahm, pointed to the contrast between the cranberries' sharp, sour flavor and the richness of the chocolate. It's the same reason tart fruit and chocolate can work so well together, even if cranberry sauce isn't exactly the first thing you'd think to dip.

The limited-edition chocolates are available exclusively at Compartés for $24.95 per four-pack, while supplies last, with the gourmet chocolate brand also making chocolate turkeys filled with Ocean Spray's whole-berry cranberry sauce in both milk and dark chocolate options.

Cranberry sauce might never get the same love as mashed potatoes, but chocolate certainly gives it a fighting chance.

#6582. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Caroline Deroche Pasquier joins Dior in a newly created role as director of press, VIP and cultural relations. She began her career at Saint Laurent before joining LVMH, where she worked at Louis Vuitton and Givenchy. During the last six years, Pasquier has led global communications for Bottega Veneta and then Versace. At Dior, she will work closely with the house’s creative director Jonathan Anderson, reporting to Olivier Bialobos, deputy managing director in charge of global communication and image.

Company comments: “[Deroche Pasquier’s] career spans communication, creative collaboration, international markets and cultural relationships, giving her a broad perspective on the development and expression of luxury brands,” the company said in a statement.

Background: Oliver Timm has voluntarily stepped down from Hugo Boss, where he’s been both chief sales officer and deputy CEO since 2024, as well as the company board. In the meantime, CEO Daniel Grieder, alongside CFO and COO Ivica Maric, will split Timm’s previous duties. Timm was initially appointed as chief sales officer in 2021, to oversee Hugo Boss’s two brands (Boss and Hugo), including wholesale, e-commerce, visual merchandizing, retail operations, and customer relations.

The announcement follows Hugo Boss’s 5% sales drop in Q3 — attributed to an ongoing turnaround at the company — and Frasers Group’s de-facto takeover of the company on October 23.

Company comments: “Oliver Timm and I have been working side by side throughout our careers for almost 30 years, and it is a great honor for me to look back on this time and the many moments we have shared. I will miss working alongside him,” said Grieder in a statement. “During his time at Hugo Boss, he has repositioned sales with a future-oriented omnichannel approach and a strong customer-centric mindset, making a significant contribution to our growth and digitalization. As I look back at these achievements, I wish him, also on behalf of the entire managing board, the very best for the future.”

Michael Murray, Hugo Boss chair and Frasers Group CEO, also shared his appreciation: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Oliver Timm for his contribution to Hugo Boss over the past years. We appreciate his commitment and wish him all the best for his professional and personal future.”

Background: Ben Hallam, most recently SVP of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, has been appointed as Lululemon’s chief brand officer. At the sportswear brand, Hallam will lead global brand marketing, brand creative, store experience, and community. He will join the company’s senior leadership team and report to CEO Heidi O’Neill who joined in April 2026.

The announcement comes after the appointments of Maggie Gauger as president and chief product officer and Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. On Friday, the company also announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective November 23. Sunderland joins from Boston Consulting Group and will report to chief financial officer Meghan Frank. Searches remain underway for a chief technology officer and a chief communications officer.

Company comments: “Ben brings an exceptional combination of creative vision, commercial discipline, and experience transforming iconic, premium brands at scale,” O’Neill said in a statement. “His proven ability to translate brand strategy into distinctive and compelling guest experiences will be critical as we strengthen how our brand comes to life across every touchpoint. Ben will play a central role in building a stronger and more competitive Lululemon.”

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business. At Pucci, Boissonnas will strengthen the brand’s distinctive creative identity, desirability, and international reach, while reporting to Pietro Beccari, chair and CEO of the LVMH Fashion Group. As for Saar Debrouwere, who has led Pucci since 2022, her future role will be announced in due course, according to the group.

Company comments: “Clara has made a significant contribution to Louis Vuitton through her deep product expertise, strong creative sensibility, and unwavering commitment to excellence. Her ability to combine creative ambition with a clear understanding of the business makes her ideally suited to lead Pucci into its next chapter,” Beccari said in a statement.

Background: Yanina Novitskaya, who has spent the last 19 years at Cartier, most recently as CEO of South East Asia and Oceania, is the next chief executive of Richemont-owned Delvaux. Delvaux, the world’s oldest fine leather goods house, was founded in Brussels in 1829. In its next chapter, Novitskaya succeeds Jean-Marc Loubier, who returned to lead the brand after its acquisition in 2021, and will report to Richemont fashion and accessories CEO Philippe Fortunado.

Company comments: “Yanina’s strong knowledge of the luxury industry will be instrumental in leading Delvaux into its next chapter, strengthening its distinctive positioning and continuing to drive product desirability and international growth,” Fortunato said in a statement.

Background: Marc Jacobs has appointed John Wattiker as CMO to lead the brand’s global marketing strategy. Wattiker joins the brand after almost 15 years at Hearst Magazines working in the company’s advertising business, where he most recently held the role of VP of fashion and luxury. Prior to Hearst, he worked in the banking sector. At Marc Jacobs, Wattiker will oversee efforts to strengthen brand positioning, deepen consumer engagement and further expand the recently acquired brand’s global reach and relevance under new owner WHP Global.

Company comments: “John brings deep experience across luxury, fashion and media, with a clear understanding of how to build brands and engage consumers,” Marc Jacobs CEO Eric Marechalle said in a statement. “He pairs creative instinct with strategic and commercial discipline and brings an extensive network of relationships built over the course of his career. I am confident he will be a great addition to our leadership team as we grow Marc Jacobs globally.”

Background: Chanel has appointed a creative makeup director, Lucia Pieroni. Previously, Pieroni was creative director of makeup at Shiseido-owned Clé de Peau Beauté (2006-2019), which led to a series of partnerships with photographers and designers where Pieroni helped shape beauty direction for fashion shows, editorials, and campaigns. At Chanel, she will work alongside the makeup creation studio reporting to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty.

Company comments: “Lucia possesses an extraordinary instinct for beauty. She perceives the individuality in every face and understands with precision how to reveal it, creating makeup that feels intuitive and expressive, while always celebrating singularity. Her artistic vision and unique savoir-faire will make this collaboration a decisive new chapter for Chanel Makeup,” Cattaneo said in a statement.

Background: Alistair McCallum, formerly global communications VP at Burberry, has been appointed chief marketing officer of Givenchy. McCallum arrives with international comms experience at fellow LVMH house Fendi, and before that, at Alexander McQueen, where he worked with now-Givenchy creative director Sarah Burton. He will report to brand CEO Amandine Ohayon.

Company comments: “The arrival of Alistair McCallum [...] on our executive committee brings recognized expertise in the luxury and fashion worlds to support our international ambition and teams worldwide,” Ohayon said in a statement.

Background: LVMH-owned jewelry brand Repossi has appointed Matthieu Soudan as managing director. The hire comes as the brand’s former CEO Anne de Vergeron returns to her management responsibilities at the LVMH group level. Soudan has been in the LVMH ecosystem for nine years, the majority of which were spent as general manager of Tag Heuer before moving to Bvlgari in 2025. At Repossi, he will lead the brand into its next phase within the world of contemporary high jewelry, while strengthening its positioning and global reach.

Company comments: “I am delighted to entrust the leadership of Repossi to Matthieu Soudan as we open a new chapter in the development of this distinctive maison. At Tag Heuer and more recently at Bvlgari, he has demonstrated a strong strategic vision, together with the ability to execute strategies that support operational excellence and the desirability of our maisons,” Stéphane Bianchi, group managing director and CEO of LVMH Watches & Jewelry, said in a statement.

Background: Capri has appointed Catherine So as the company’s chief legal and sustainability officer. So joins from Tiffany & Co., where she most recently served as senior vice president and general counsel, where she oversaw legal, compliance, intellectual property, litigation, governance and brand protection. She spent 15 years at Tiffany across various roles.

Company comments: “We are pleased to welcome Catherine to Capri Holdings. She is a highly respected legal leader with extensive experience with helping develop global luxury brands and executive teams through periods of transformation and growth,” CEO John D. Idol said in a statement. “Her expertise, leadership, and strategic perspective will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our business and position our brands for long-term success.”

Background: Poshmark has made a string of executive hires. Creative consultant Jamie Hunter, who worked as a buyer and fashion director at Bergdorf Goodman, has been appointed fashion and creative director of the California-based resale company. This new role signals Poshmark’s ambition to become an authority in the fashion resale space, by bringing its curation, styling and creative direction in-house, informed by Hunter’s two-plus decades in the industry.

Other new hires include: Yoshitaka Matsuzawa as SVP of seller and community experience, leading product development across consumer experiences and AI; Kishore Kumar Mohan (formerly The RealReal) as engineering SVP; Lesley Clifford as VP of merchandising, also a new role supporting a more strategic approach to assortment and brand relationships; and Beth Newman (formerly Canada Goose) as PR and communications director.

Company comments: “We’ve been deliberate about bringing in leaders who add deep expertise in their respective fields and fresh perspectives to Poshmark. With experience spanning fashion, technology and retail, they’re strengthening our leadership team and helping us sharpen our fashion point of view,” chief revenue officer Elizabeth von der Goltz said in a statement.

Background: Stephan Sturm has decided to step down as chair and member of the supervisory board of Hugo Boss, following discussions between the brand and its now-largest shareholder Frasers Group. The Mike Ashley-owned business upped its stake in the German brand in mid-August, from 30.28%% to 47.89%; the rising share comes on the heels of Frasers’s June takeover bid of £1.72 billion, which the Hugo Boss board deemed “inadequate” and urged shareholders to reject.

Now the largest shareholder of the Hugo Boss business, Frasers Group is edging closer to expanding to its portfolio further, following the acquisition of UK department store Harvey Nichols last month. Sturm will continue to serve as chair until a successor has been elected.

Company comments: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Stephan Sturm for his leadership, commitment, and dedication to Hugo Boss. We respect his decision and will work closely with him to ensure a smooth transition,” deputy chair Sinan Piskin said in a statement.

Background: Space NK has named Emma Simpson-Scott as CEO, succeeding Andy Lightfoot, who is stepping down after a decade heading the beauty retailer. Following a period of significant growth and transformation, including its recent acquisition by Ulta Beauty, Simpson-Scott will now lead the business as it matures further. Previously, the executive spent seven and a half years as CMO and 10 years at Space NK altogether.

Company comments: “Under Andy’s leadership, Space NK achieved significant growth, strengthened its position as a market-leading beauty retailer, and successfully transitioned into the Ulta Beauty family,” Kecia Steelman, president CEO of parent company Ulta Beauty, said in a statement. “Emma is a highly respected retail leader who brings deep customer insight, retail expertise and a passion for building exceptional teams. I look forward to our continued work together as she leads Space NK into the next chapter of growth.”

Background: Southern Californian brand St. John has named former co-creative director of Kenzo Humberto Leon as creative director. Beyond Kenzo, Leon co-founded fashion concept store Opening Ceremony in 2002 and is best known for his distinctive multidisciplinary approach to design. At St. John, Leon will oversee the knitwear brand’s image, design, and overall creative direction.

Company comments: “Humberto brings a rare instinct for honoring our history while making it feel entirely new. He understands that true luxury lives in how clothing makes people feel, which is the very spirit Marie Gray built this house on. Together, we’re introducing St. John to a new generation who may not have felt it was made for them until now,” CEO Mandy West said in a statement.

Background: Richemont has appointed Anton Rupert as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board. Rupert, the son of Richemont chair Johann Rupert, has served as a non-executive director on Richemont’s board since 2017. He served as director of Watchfinder from July 2018 until December 2019. Since January 2021, he has served on the advisory board of Asia Partners Fund LP I, a regional Southeast Asia private equity fund focused on growth-stage technology-based opportunities. Following the meeting of Richemont’s board of directors on September 8, Richemont announced his appointment as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board of directors. He will serve alongside Bram Schot, who was appointed non-executive deputy chair in 2024 and who will continue in his role.

Company comments: “This appointment is an important step in the board’s long-term succession planning,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said in a statement. “Richemont’s strength has always rested on the continuity that comes from close family involvement, on rigorous governance, and on an unwavering commitment to creativity and craftsmanship. Having Anton and Bram serve together as non-executive co-deputy chairmen ensures that each of these foundations is given the attention it deserves: Anton will continue to safeguard the creative and product priorities that define our maisons, while Bram will ensure that our governance remains of the highest standard.”

Background: James Kelly has been named CEO of Theory, after joining the brand in 2022 as CFO and later as global co-chief operating officer. As global CEO of both Theory and Helmut Lang, Kelly will oversee both brands’ headquarters functions, commercial operations, and global growth initiatives. Before joining Theory, Kelly helped scale Uniqlo’s US expansion. He succeeds Dinesh Tandon, who will transition into the co-chief operating officer role, as well as returning to his role as CEO of Theory China.

Company comments: “James has been an instrumental leader for Theory over the past several years, bringing strategic vision, operational excellence and a deep understanding of our business,” said Kazumi Yanai, chairman of Theory. “As James assumes the role of global CEO and Dinesh focuses his leadership on one of our most important markets, we are further expanding our global organization and positioning Theory for continued success around the world.”

Background: Charlotte Fournet, the niece of Kering chair François-Henri Pinault, has been named CEO of jewelry maison Pomellato, succeeding Kering Italia president Sabina Belli. Fournet joined Saint Laurent in 2014 before moving to Gucci in 2019 and then Bottega Veneta in 2020, where she climbed the merchandising ladder to become director just over three years ago. Krizia Cucurachi, who joined Dodo in 2024 as global product and brand director, has been promoted to CEO. Prior to joining the brand, she spent more than a decade at Swarovski across several senior leadership positions. Both will report to Kering Jewelry CEO Jean-Marc Duplaix, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Jewelry is a strategic growth pillar for Kering. Pomellato and Dodo are two highly distinctive houses with strong identities and tremendous potential. Charlotte’s extensive experience across several Kering houses and Krizia’s strong track record in brand-building and transformation make them ideally positioned to lead the next phase of growth for Pomellato and Dodo,” Duplaix said in a statement.

Background: Sabina Belli, who joined Kering as CEO of Pomellato in 2015, has been named president of Kering Italia. Before joining the French luxury group, Belli held senior marketing and executive roles at WPP, L’Oréal Luxe and LVMH, spanning the likes of Christian Dior Parfums, Moët Hennessy, Veuve Clicquot, and Bvlgari. Since this April, she has also led Kering Accademia per le Eccellenze, a Kering initiative dedicated to preserving and promoting Italian craftsmanship, alongside serving on the directors board of the Kering Foundation. In her new role, Belli will report directly to CEO Luca de Meo, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Italy occupies a unique place in Kering’s history, identity, and future. Its creativity, craftsmanship, and industrial excellence are at the heart of our houses and the long-term vitality of the luxury industry,” de Meo said in a statement. “Sabina brings a deep understanding of the Italian luxury ecosystem and a strong ability to build partnerships across business, education and public institutions.”

Background: Kristin Bauer, who spent three years as chief supply chain officer for sneaker retailer Foot Locker, will join Converse as chief operating officer. As parent company Nike works to revive its Converse business, following consecutive quarters of slow sales, it is rebuilding a leadership structure to help propel growth. Bauer will report to Nike COO Venky Alagirisamy.

Company comments: “We are excited to welcome Kristin and look forward to the perspective she will bring as we continue to build momentum for the brand,” Nike said in a statement.

Background: Jane Ewing has been named chief commercial officer and executive vice president of Nike, reporting directly to CEO Elliott Hill. She joins after a 14-year tenure at Walmart, most recently serving as interim CEO for Sam’s Club China. She also previously held senior leadership roles at Diageo. In her new role, Ewing will lead Nike’s global marketplace organization, including Sales and Nike Direct.

Company’s comments: “Jane’s experience, leadership and global perspective will help us continue this work and accelerate growth across Nike Direct and wholesale. Her role is vital to creating even stronger connections between brand, product and marketplace while serving athletes* and consumers around the world,” Hill said in a statement.

Background: The British Fashion Council (BFC) has announced that David Pemsel is stepping down as chair after four years in the position and 10 years on the executive board. During his time as chair, the BFC achieved record revenue figures (£14 million in FY2024/25), raised £7.2 million through the BFC Foundation and secured a multi-million-pound investment from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Pemsel also appointed Laura Weir as BFC CEO in early 2025. A successor will be announced in September.

Company comments: “David has been an exceptional chair and an unwavering champion of British fashion. His leadership has helped strengthen the British Fashion Council as an organization, creating the stability, governance and long-term foundations that enable us to deliver our ambitions for the industry,” Weir said in a statement.

Background: Alexandre Oulès has been named chief operating officer for the LVMH beauty division, reporting to Véronique Courtois, president and CEO of Parfums Christian Dior and of the LVMH Group’s beauty division. According to the internal announcement, his new role will “oversee manufacturing, supply chain, and purchasing across the beauty division, driving stronger convergence between maisons across all three functions”. Oulès joins from Balenciaga, where he was appointed COO in October 2023. He previously held roles at L’Oréal, Guerlain, Celine and Moët Hennessy.

Company’s comment: “I am delighted to welcome back Alexandre, whose pursuit of operational excellence is widely recognized. His knowledge of the group and the specificities of the beauty world will strongly contribute to the overall efficiency of our operations,” Courtois said.

Background: Maya Dukes, who previously worked at Macy’s as head of graphic design (2001-2007), will return to the retailer as executive creative director.
