#6571. Buttermilk Drop Biscuits

Recipe by Grace Vallo, Windham, New Hampshire

These buttermilk drop biscuits are tender, fluffy and buttery—no rolling, kneading or shaping required.

Buttermilk biscuits are, in my humble opinion, the perfect breakfast. They’re endlessly versatile—perfect for drowning in spicy sausage gravy, loading up with bacon and egg for a sandwich, or simply slathering with butter and jam. There’s really nothing a flaky biscuit can’t do. But I don’t always have the time or energy to roll and cut dough in the morning, and that’s where drop biscuits come in to save the day—or at least to stop me from opening up a can of refrigerated dough.

Making drop biscuits is almost improbably easy. You just stir together a few pantry staples to make the dough, plop spoonfuls on the pan and bake them until they’re perfectly golden brown. Whether you’re an experienced biscuit maker or looking to whip up your first-ever batch, this simple recipe delivers maximum payoff with just a couple of simple ingredients and a little bit of effort.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. As the oven warms up, combine the flour, baking soda, baking powder and salt in a large mixing bowl.

Editor’s Tip: Use a fork or a whisk to give the ingredients a good stir to make sure they’re all evenly incorporated.

Using a pastry cutter or a fork, cut the chilled butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

Editor’s Tip: You could use your hands to incorporate the butter into the flour, but use a light touch. The heat from your hands can melt the butter, and you don’t want that!

Stir the buttermilk into the crumb mixture just until it’s moistened.

Editor’s Tip: Grab your buttermilk straight from the refrigerator so it’s nice and cold. Mix just until you’ve formed a shaggy dough. It’s OK if your dough looks a little bit lumpy—you don’t want to over-mix it!

Drop the dough by 1/4-cupfuls 2 inches apart onto a greased baking sheet. Bake the biscuits until they’re golden brown on top, 11 to 13 minutes. Serve warm with butter, if desired.

Editor’s Tip: Don’t worry about making them perfectly round. A little bit of irregularity is part of the fun of drop biscuits.

Drop biscuits tend to be best right out of the oven, but you can place any leftovers inside an airtight storage container, where they’ll last on the counter for three to five days. Heat the biscuits up in a 200° oven for 5 to 10 minutes to bring them back to life.

There are several buttermilk substitutes, and the easiest one—white vinegar—is probably already in your pantry. Add 1 tablespoon of white vinegar to a 1-cup measure, then fill it the rest of the way with cold milk.

Make it a 3-ingredient recipe by swapping self-rising flour for the all-purpose flour. You won’t need the baking powder or the baking soda, as they’re already included in the flour mix. Mix the flour with the butter and buttermilk as directed to create an even easier batch of drop biscuits.

If your buttermilk drop biscuits are dense, check your baking powder. It’s possible that it’s expired, which could mean that it was too weak to help your dough rise. You may have also overworked the dough, which can result in a dense, tough biscuit.

#6570. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

#6568. How New York and L.A. Celebrated Diwali in Style

Diwali—which translates to “festival of lights”—fêted by the global South Asian diaspora is a five-day celebration that began on Friday, November 6, a date decided by the Hindu lunar calendar. Diwali marks the new year, brings the promise of prosperity, and signifies the triumph of good over evil. While customs range across religion and region, the festival often means dedicating hours to baking sweets and lighting an unfathomable number of tea light candles, as well as giving up meat, fish, and alcohol. There’s also the deep cleaning rituals—to make room for blessings.

But in the U.S., more epicurean customs have emerged, which means weeks of parties, dinners, and gatherings in the lead-up. It’s proving to be a loophole for more indulgent fanfare before the official start of Diwali. Here’s Vogue’s look inside the celebrations everyone was talking about this year.

“Look around, look out the windows: We’re in New York City,” Jessel Taank told the crowd gathered at Boom at the Standard High Line. For the ŌUSHQ founder and Real Housewives of New York star, this soirée was one she had been dreaming of for some time. “On January 1st I wrote in my little notebook, ‘Host Diwali at The Standard’ as it was something I really wanted to do,” she said. “Growing up, Diwali was more of an intimate, community thing and what it’s become is so extraordinary.”

For the second annual Diwali Noir party presented by the fashion platform in partnership with the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Taank was joined on hosting duty by Prakti Beauty founder and model Pritika Swarup and the CFDA’s Marc Karimzadeh.

The high-octane evening invited guests to embrace an “Indian-inspired” dress code. “We really wanted to crush the stereotypes, because when you think of Indian fashion it is really occasionwear-heavy, big lehenga cupcakes, and embellishments,” Taank told Vogue. “I don't think Indian fashion is like that anymore. There’s a lot of creative energy coming from the Middle East and India that doesn’t get enough credit and recognition.”

Taank wore a metallic and bejeweled chocolate gown by Prabal Gurung, while Swarup opted for a bright punch-pink floor-length Rahul Mishra dress. “Look at everyone here tonight,” Swarup chimed in. “We wanted them to have their own interpretation of what modern Indian fashion is—and everyone looks incredible.”

Jenna Lyons donned sunglasses and an all-black ensemble topped with a bow, designer Sami Miro adorned herself in jewels from luxury Indian brand Outhouse, and mother-daughter duo Rachel Roy and Ava Dash took traditional Indian garments—palazzo pants and baroque blouses—and played with silhouettes, adding plumes of crimson fur and a flash of midriff.

While Diwali was the reason for the celebration, the night itself felt like an exercise in cultural exchange and discovery. Guests included Daniel Boulud, Bibhu Mohapatra, Kate Davidson Hudson, Katya Tolstova, Madhulika Sharma, Ankur Jain, Carly Cushnie, Ronny Kobo, Michelle Ochs, Roopal Patel, Dhaval Bhanusali, Azeezah Khan, Natalie De’Banco, Priya Shukla, Jay Sean, Akbar Hamid, and Junaid Mahmood, alongside Taank’s fellow cast members Sai De Silva, Erika Hammond, and Devyn Simone.

The evening also marked the official re-launch of ŌUSHQ’s multi-brand e-commerce website and the introduction of its new editorial destination dedicated to fashion, culture, and designer discovery. Behind the bar, towers of Johnnie Walker Blue Label bottles spiraled towards the ceiling as bartenders whipped up martinis, margaritas, and poured countless glasses of Champagne. Hammond and De Silva sipped cocktails and giggled with Miro, while stylist Micaela Erlanger perched at the end of the bar with Natasha Das, founder of Danarys, who nibbled on spicy bites of lamb, and morsels like samosas and pakora. “Diwali is quickly becoming one of my favorite party seasons,” Erlanger quipped.

On the other side of the room, the dance floor heaved, as Bollywood favorites like the 1999 hit “Dilbar” blended with Afro tech, while the Egyptian hit “Ah Ya Albi” played alongside Keinemusik’s “Move.” The music paused once briefly to give way to dancers who, atop the bar, performed a routine that, much like the dress code, blended India and the West.

“Can I just say, I don’t remember the last time I was in a room with so many beautiful people and so many beautifully dressed people,” added Karimzadeh, senior director of content and communications at the CFDA. “This is amazing.”

As speeches concluded, the party loosened further, turning from a bustling soiree to an all-out “rager”—to quote Taank. EDM and hip-hop boomed through the speakers, drinks spilled, dresses were trampled on, and by 1 a.m. the Champagne eventually ran out.

“We take for granted that the journey from gas to dust to protostar to star to supernova takes more than just a miracle—it takes time,” Gold House executive chairman and CEO Bing Chen shared in his remarks at The Majestic Downtown. It was a fitting metaphor for what Gold House called its largest Gold Diwali yet.

The organization threw its celebration for the Festival of Lights in Los Angeles, marking both its expansion as an institution and Diwali’s growing relevance. “Diwali is a celebration of light, community, and connection, and we wanted to bring that spirit to our Gold Diwali while honoring how culture shapes who we are and the possibilities we create,” Chen said.

The event began with the cast and producers of Ramayana: Part 1: Rise of a Legend introducing themselves and the film, released on November 5, which has already grossed over $56 million at the box office. It is also the most expensive film to be made in the region.

Gold House met the moment and announced a new partnership with nonprofit film fund South Stack Studios to launch the Gold Stack Shorts Fund, supporting short films and micro-series focused on South Asian stories.

The crowd, which was a bustling gathering of prominent entertainers, CEOs, and creators, brought together the likes of Freida Pinto, Tan France, Hannah Simone, Avantika, Dhar Mann, Richa Moorjani, and Rhea Raj, as well as Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash, Poshmark founder Manish Chandra, and Anita Chatterjee.

Many attendees stuck to tradition, with jewel-toned lehengas, statement jewelry, saris, and bright sherwanis, but some played around with patent corsets in place of blouses and mini skirts.

Around the room, orange and golden marigolds were arranged in big, lush clusters with tropical palm fronds and brass lanterns. Friends, old and new, came together and enjoyed Diwali customs: Some grazed on a South Asian menu by Rasoi Catering, many danced as DJ MissNINJA performed with a live tabla performance, and others congregated in a dedicated Carrom Game Lounge where they played the traditional board game.

Indian luxury designer Anita Dongre debuted a one-off carrom board, painted by hand in collaboration with Gold House, that recontextualizes the tabletop game as a contemporary design object. Also on display was the Cuyana x Gold House Marigold Charm, a limited-edition piece released earlier in October.

Indian fashion house Sabyasachi’s multi-year collaboration with The Metropolitan Museum culminated in his first New York show in almost 20 years. So hosting the first Diwali party of its kind inside the hallowed halls of the storied institution, in many ways, felt fated.

“Ever since New York started having an official Diwali calendar, I wanted to host a party—and what could be a better venue than this,” designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee told Vogue. “It’s so iconic and it’s so New York. I think people are excited about this, so I’m very honored.”

Inside the American Wing’s Charles Engelhard Court, a crowd gathered to show off their opulent garments, from sleek sherwanis and richly textured shalwar kameez to sequined dresses and sharply tailored suits. Close friends of the designer, like Anjula Acharia, Jessel Taank, and Micaela Erlanger, all wore head-to-toe Sabyasachi looks, right down to the jewelry.

Guests in attendance included Kal Penn, Amy Fine Collins, Fern Mallis, Rhea Raj, Romilly Newman, Alioune Badara Fall, Nell Rebowe, Shruti Ganguly, Marie Ecot, Merritt Beck, Linda Fargo, Isiah Magsino, Imran Amed, Yumi Shin, Jully Patel, Angelica Hicks, and Carlos Mota.

As a six-piece band rattled off sultry renditions of songs like Dean Martin’s “Sway,” attendees were greeted with silver trays of Dom Pérignon Champagne and Petrossian caviar. Though most ended up mesmerized by what stood in the center of the room: A spectacular 16-foot-long grazing table, which was more like a culinary cornucopia outfitted with a peacock and an astounding bloom of ranunculus, roses, peonies, and winterberries. On offer, towering croquembouches, meringues, decadent cakes, and overflowing displays of fine chocolates and Indian sweets were placed alongside a lavish raw bar of fresh Maine lobster and oysters, fine Iberico ham, and endless types of cheese.

As Bollywood actress Rani Mukerji and designer Waris Ahluwalia eagerly posed for photos with Sabyasachi, excited brides-to-be lined up to introduce themselves to the designer, brimming with equal parts awe and nerves. Other guests sipped on spiced margaritas—which seems to be the emerging signature cocktail of the Diwali season—and lounged by the fountains.

Once the drinks dwindled and the band packed up, guests slowly made their way outside, reluctant to end the glamorous night. As everyone spilled out onto the iconic Met steps, a few who glittered even in the darkness of the crisp fall night beckoned for one more photo. For some, this was just another swanky party in Manhattan, but for those who grew up celebrating Diwali, it was a night for the history books.

Buzzy Indian restaurant the Ambassador’s Clubhouse turned Manhattan’s NoMad into a vibrant hub of revelry, as Anjula Acharia welcomed an exclusive guest list to her glitzy annual black-tie ball. “So many of you didn’t get plus ones,” she quipped over the mic. “So it means that all of you have to talk to everybody.”

The beloved All That Glitters Diwali Ball once again celebrated South Asian excellence, presented in partnership with Lexus. Guests in attendance included Avantika Vandanapu, Jay Sean, Rhea Raj, Bela Bajaria, Jessel Taank, Aasif Mandvi, Poorna Jagannathan, Mira Nair, Amrit Kaur, Nimesh Patel, Sheena Melwani, designers Falguni and Shane Peacock, and Revolve’s Divya Mathur.

“Tonight is my love letter to New York and all the South Asians here that are rising and thriving,” Acharia said. “So many of you have been grinding for decades. This is a celebration of all the work that you do for our community and for yourselves. I’m just so proud to honor all of you and I really mean that from the bottom of my heart.”

New York’s sudden cold snap was no match for the glamour that was put on show. Outside, some braved the cold for a Rhudeva scent station that offered engraved bottles of perfumes, including Dusky Diwali with notes of saffron, salted pistachio, and sandalwood. Inside, the room was a smorgasbord of crimson, as red flowers layered every surface from floor to ceiling.

As guests cozied up, sipping on piquant negronis, lassi-flavored cocktails, and martinis, bright plates of Punjabi food were passed around. Think: Wagyu-infused naan and lamb curry to samosas and spiced bites of goat. Subtlety was not on the menu, nor was it the dress code. Feathers trailed behind glittery saris, sequins caught the candlelight, and silk pooled and swished, while jhumkas and bangles clinked as Calvin Harris, Burna Boy, Charli XCX, and Vishal Dadlani boomed through the speakers.

“This is a far cry from the Diwaliis that I used to host myself, 20 or 30 years ago on Riverside Drive,” filmmaker Mira Nair told the crowd. “We are all here to be counted for, to be seen, and to be actually celebrating ourselves and our amazing community, that finally is visible in the most powerful of ways.”

East met West, as Jagannathan opted for South Asian designer Rahul Mishra in an untraditional rendition of desi opulence. Taank took a more modern route, and revealed her back tattoo with a pearlescent Tarun Tahiliani halter gown, while actress Avantika stuck with tradition in a warm copper lehenga and clutched onto a Coach Tabby purse.

For everyone in attendance, more was, well, more. Acharia floated across the room in a gilded silver Falguni Shane Peacock train adorned with feather cuffs, and Raj also tapped the designer for a custom magenta feathered two-piece that felt fitting for the rising pop star.

As the dance floor got warmed up (and subsequently didn’t stop until after 1 a.m.), Anita Chatterjee, founder of A-Game Public Relations, recalled: “Years ago, I remember being in Anjula’s Tribeca loft, where she put together a small Diwali party. Back then, she told me: ‘One day, everyone's gonna know about Diwali. There's going to be so many parties, and that’s what I want. I want our holiday and what we do to be seen by all.’ Anjula: mission accomplished. We did it!”

Passerine co-founders Maneesh K. Goyal and Alvina Patel Buxani shut down their Flatiron restaurant and set the scene for an early Diwali celebration with their second annual A Luminous Table dinner.

The gathering, which also raised funds for the Asian American Writers’ Workshop, was co-hosted by filmmaker Mira Nair, journalist Radhika Jones, and novelist Salman Rushdie.

A crowd from across fashion, finance, politics, and art convened, including Tamron Hall, Aasif Mandvi and B.D. Wong, Bibhu Mohapatra, Waris Ahluwalia, Alok Vaid-Menon, and June Ambrose, who eschewed her signature statement hat for sparkles and silk.

In true desi style, guests wore bright splashes of color, embellished lehengas, and luxurious saris, filling the air with soft metallic pops of bangles and jhumkas. Those without traditional outfits reveled in color, sparkles, and sequins. After all, it’s one of the few times all-black is considered a faux pas in New York City.

After a cocktail reception with plenty of Moët Hennessy on offer, a family-style dinner was served by executive Chef Gaurav Bathla. Guests took their seats at tables laden with bud vases of tulips, hyacinths, and carnations and quickly made introductions. Ambrose shook hands with Zara Rahim, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s senior advisor, Rushdie and Italian artist Francesco Clemente chatted over red wine, and art curator Racquel Chevremont and her fiancé Mel Corpus made fast friends with their seat mates.

Siblings and friends were purposefully separated, as were some couples. “I created the seating chart that way intentionally,” Buxani told Vogue. “I wanted to create new friends so I separated some old ones. I think I have a good idea of who would get along.”

The food forged connections too. Starters like Goan chicken cafreal, Tamil shrimp Chettinad, and a samosa in Levantine katafi were quickly devoured, followed by baskets of naan and rice and a short rib pot pie filled with Old Delhi nihari, plumes of steam escaping from under its laminated pastry when theatrically cracked into.

Community was the guiding principle of the night, as co-hosts shared their stories of how Diwali offered respite as they navigated identity, immigration, and religion.

“When I was growing up in Bombay, the festivals were for all of us. It didn’t matter if we were Hindu, Muslim, Parsi—Diwali was ours,” Rushdie shared. “We all celebrated everything. And I think that this spirit is alive in this gathering.”

The celebrated novelist also noted that this energy is no longer part of the India he once knew.“There is something going on in India right now. India is boiling. And I would feel wrong not to say, maybe it’s not the thing to say in a restaurant, to celebrate the cockroach. But the young people of India have given us the most hopeful moment for a very long time.”

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is a propulsive Gen Z political movement in India that emerged earlier this year, using protests and demonstrations to demand government accountability, transparency, and major reforms across employment, education, and elections. Some have even referred to it as the Mamdani effect.

“I’m here as a mama cockroach,” Nair announced to the room to raucous cheers and applause, as the room swelled at the mention of her son, Zohran Mamdani. “Happy Diwali to all of us who believe in change. God knows the Cockroach Janta Party is reminding us that it is not enough to be quiet, it is not enough to celebrate, it is not enough to cease to question.” Her speech culminated in the room serenading her with a surprise birthday singalong.

As hot sticky date puddings covered in jaggery caramel filled the tables, Goyal stood for one last announcement. “In the old school tradition of people who live above their bodegas or restaurants, my husband and I, we live above this restaurant. There’s an after-hang at our apartment upstairs, and whether you come for 10 minutes or for two hours, everybody’s welcome. And let’s be honest, we’re New Yorkers. We like to see each other’s apartments!”

As the last sips of chili margaritas and tomato martinis were polished off, people slowly began heading for the door, and onwards to Goyal’s apartment for one more drink, one more story, and to make one more friend.

#6567. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6565. Spiced and Glazed Roast Turkey

Our mission: A roast turkey that’s boldly spiced, beautifully glazed, and—can we type this loudly enough?—PROPERLY COOKED. That means juicy breast meat, tender dark meat, and plenty of deeply browned skin. Andy Baraghani and Brad Leone’s solution? Break the bird into five pieces: two wings, two legs, and one whole breast. Roasting the bird in parts gives you more control over when each piece is done—no dry breast meat or tough legs.

They didn’t slouch on flavor either. A peppery dry brine with garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika gets to work 24–48 hours before the turkey goes into the oven. Then comes the glaze: a savory-tangy mix of soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, orange zest, and herbs. Brushed onto the turkey as it roasts, it builds a glossy, deeply burnished finish. And because the pieces cook on a wire rack set inside a baking sheet, you get more exposed skin for browning and a more even cook overall.

If the idea of doing surgery on a raw turkey gives you a stress rash, ask your butcher to do it—even at the supermarket. Request a 12–14-lb. turkey cut into five pieces, with the thighs attached to the drumsticks, the breast left whole, and the backbone removed. If they ask why, just say: Yes, you’re making that ridiculous Bon Appétit recipe. If you’d rather do the honors yourself, here’s our guide to breaking down a whole turkey.

Choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. Many supermarket birds are already treated with a salt solution, sometimes labeled “self-basting,” “enhanced,” or “contains a solution.” Adding this dry brine on top can make the turkey overly salty. Check the packaging before you buy.

Should I rinse off the dry brine before roasting?

No. Leave the seasoning on the turkey when you coat it with oil. Some of the spice mixture may rub off, but that’s fine. There’s no need to rinse the bird, and washing raw poultry can spread bacteria around your kitchen.

Can I use the pan drippings to make gravy?

Yes, but taste them first. Between the seasoned dry brine and soy-based glaze, the drippings can be quite salty and intensely flavored. Use them sparingly and taste your gravy before adding more salt. For a simpler option, try our Make-Ahead Gravy, which doesn’t require drippings at all.

Read our guide to turkey cooking times, no matter the bird’s size or your preferred cooking method.

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 24 hours dry-brining

Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck and giblets removed, breast side up, on a cutting board and pat dry. Grip a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate the wing from the breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get into the place where the joint meets the socket). Remove wing; repeat on the other side.

Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until the ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through the joint to separate leg. Repeat on the other side.

Now for the breast: Position the turkey breast side down with the opening facing you. Using kitchen shears, cut along one side of backbone until you get all the way through the neck end, then turn the turkey 180° and cut through the other side to remove the backbone (save it for making stock).

Very finely grind 2 Tbsp. whole black peppercorns and 2 Tbsp. whole pink or black peppercorns in a spice mill or mortar and pestle; transfer to a medium bowl. Add ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. garlic powder, 2 Tbsp. onion powder, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1 Tbsp. smoked paprika, and use your fingers to mix together.

Place turkey pieces, skin side up, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. Sprinkle salt mixture liberally all over turkey, patting to adhere. You may not need all of it, but it’s good to have extra since some will end up on the baking sheet. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 24 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil to make cleanup easy and set rack back inside. Arrange turkey pieces on rack, skin side up, and let sit at room temperature up to 2 hours to help decrease the cooking time.

Meanwhile, cook small handful of hardy herbs (such as sage, rosemary, bay leaves, and/or thyme), 4 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, ⅓ cup low-sodium soy sauce, ⅓ cup (packed; 71 g) light brown sugar, and ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until sugar is dissolved and glaze thickens slightly (it should just barely coat a spoon), 10–12 minutes. Remove glaze from heat.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Rub turkey with 6 Tbsp. neutral oil (such as vegetable, peanut, or canola) and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet. Roast turkey, rotating baking sheet halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown, 20–25 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 20 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast registers 150°, and 170° when inserted into the thickest part of the thighs, 50–70 minutes longer (total cooking time will be 1–1½ hours). Skin should be deep golden brown and shiny. Transfer turkey to a cutting board; tent loosely with foil. Let rest 30–60 minutes before carving.

Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published in our November 2019 issue. We’ve updated the introduction with additional cooking guidance and answers to common reader questions; we’ve also updated the recipe for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving recipes →

#6563. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6562. Mocha Brown Hair-Color Season Is Here—and It’s Universally Flattering

There’s something about this time of year that makes everybody want to go darker. From their nail polish to their wardrobe, it’s a turn toward rich, darker shades. So it’s only natural that hair color would follow suit, going deeper and darker too. This winter in particular, it’s all about mocha brown.

Also called mocha chocolate, the rich, glossy shade was first popularized by celebrity colorist Jenna Perry, whose multidimensional brunette wizardry has fans like Bella Hadid and Kaia Gerber. Since then, the smooth and chocolaty hue—which combines darker espresso tones with lighter, milkier brunette shades—has become popular with a much wider section of the A-list, with Hailey Bieber and Daisy Edgar-Jones among the latest devotees.

“It reminds me of a chocolate mousse or a rich chocolate cake,” Perry tells Vogue. “That’s where the name came from. I thought mocha chocolate resembled the decadence of this shade of brown.” In line with sweater weather, Perry has churned out individualized takes on what she calls the “universally flattering brunette hair color” for a slew of stars, including longtime client Emily Ratajkowski and Amelia Gray. “A deep, rich brunette is chic,” Perry says. “The color reflects warmly in the sun, so it doesn’t ever look drab.”

According to Stephen Buller and Anita Rice, founders of Buller and Rice salon, these cacao tones feel luxurious for winter, particularly when the color isn’t completely flat. The key? Having a varied tone. “This is important throughout the lengths and ends so it reflects light and feels expensive rather than looking like one solid block of dark color,” they say. “This also gives clients who have had years of balayage an opportunity to go darker without feeling as though they’re simply covering everything up.”

Celebrity hairstylist Lorraine Dublin says that these indulgent, chocolaty shades look especially beautiful on textured and curly hair: “Think deep espresso brown with subtle ribbons of mocha, creating a rich, multidimensional finish,” she previously told Vogue. “It works beautifully on textured hair because the tonal variations catch the light, highlighting the shape and movement of curls, coils, and kinks.” She recommends asking your colorist for a “rich espresso base” with “delicate mocha or cinnamon brown accents,” which will impart a soft, seamless color melt.

Another important part of mastering the mocha chocolate look is keeping hair strong and shiny. “What makes this hair color so incredible from the start is having healthy hair,” explains Perry, who adds that preserving pigments with a color-safe shampoo and conditioner is key. Try Matrix Total Results Brass Off Shampoo to nix brassy or red tones. You can also use an at-home gloss or color conditioner, like Glaze Supergloss Color Conditioning Hair Gloss Chocolate Gleam or John Frieda Brilliant Brunette Color Vibrancy Conditioner, to prolong your hair’s vibrancy.

If a rich shade of mocha chocolate sounds like a delectable prospect, discover even more mocha brown hair-color inspiration to take to your salon below.

#6560. I’m So Obsessed With This Coffee Mug, I Tell Strangers About It

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

#6559. Inside Designer Carla Fernández’s Vibrant Mexico City Home, Full of Indigenous Textiles and Art

When the Mexico City–based writer and curator Su Wu started working on her new design book, a theme began to emerge: She kept noticing the presence of pre-Hispanic architectural and design traditions in modern Mexican interiors.

It was from this realization that Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes was born. The book features 16 homes across Mexico—those of artists, architects, designers, and more—all shot by photographer Luis Garvan.

Wrought iron doors designed by Carla Fernández.

“When I began this project, I thought that we would be documenting a history, like the aura surrounding the artifacts in a museum, the apparitions of the past,” Wu writes in the book’s introduction. “Instead, what I’ve found is the vibrant, living presence of Indigenous ideas in Mexico.”

“In the guest bedroom, pink silk curtains dyed by Fernández cast a glow in the room. The bedspread is from her personal collection of Mesoamerican textiles, made of undyed wool in Teotitlán del Valle, Oaxaca.”—Su Wu

One space that exemplifies those ideas is Casa Flora, the colorful brutalist Mérida home and studio of the Mexican fashion designer Carla Fernández. As a designer, Fernández seeks to preserve the textile traditions of Indigenous and Mestizo communities through collaborations with artisans, bringing ancient practices to a contemporary audience. Fittingly, the home is full of Mesoamerican art and textiles.

Fernández led the renovation of the house, which dates back more than a century and now hosts workshops for Taller Flora, her design lab, which focuses on traditional Indigenous clothing techniques. (You can also stay in the home; the designer lists it for stays on Airbnb.)

Fernández’s husband, the artist Pedro Reyes, created several elements of the space, including a concrete outdoor shower, as well as some of the tiles throughout the space. His sculptures—including a prototype of Mitla Sillas, chairs inspired by the pyramids of the Mitla archaeological site in Oaxaca—are found throughout the home.

The outdoor shower designed by Pedro Reyes.

Reflecting on Fernández’s home, Wu tells Vogue: “I was very moved when writing the book with the idea of the ‘void’ in Mesoamerican architecture, and how so many architects, going back to the writings of Teodoro González de León, described the patio as a central, defining feature of the Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and open to the elements. And in Carla’s home, I think there are many moments that exemplify this idea of the boundary between interior and exterior being not a physical one, but rather a marker of movement across psychological states.”

“A latticed window, known in Mexico as a celosia, is a central part of Mesoamerican architecture, used for cross-ventilation and to create a permeable sense of separation and shadow.”—Su Wu

Prototypes of Reyes’s Mitla Sillas chairs.

For Wu, Casa Flora is also a prime example of an idea that chef Elena Reygadas wrote about in her foreword to the book, “which is that handmade things are meant to be lived with no matter how precious, or especially if precious.”

“An equipale chair made of bent wood by the Wixárika people in Nayarit sits in front of a backstrap-loom tapestry of the Torre Latinoamericana, the iconic skyscraper in Mexico City designed by architect Augusto H. Álvarez. Made by artisans from San Juan Cancuc, Chiapas, the tapestry echoes a collection of dresses from Carla Fernández that featured historic buildings in Mexico City.”—Su Wu

All images © Luis GarvanCasa Flora, Mérida, Yucatán (pages 244-263). Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes by Su Wu. Published by Phaidon Press.

#6558. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6557. Chocolate-Covered Caramel Apple Slices Are the Easiest Treats for Fall Get-Togethers

These chocolate-covered caramel apple slices turn the fruit into a glorified candy bar. Bring them to Friendsgiving or keep them in the fridge for a quick weekday snack.

With two little girls who have been loving all things fall these past couple months, my social algorithm has been filled with cozy crafts, Halloween costume ideas, and, of course, all the seasonal treats. When I scrolled to these chocolate-covered apple slices on a stick from @Crowded kitchen, I knew my daughters would go crazy for them.

Whole, uncut candy-coated apples are too big and too difficult for them to eat, but their eyes widen with delight every time we see them in the store. That’s exactly why this tip is genius. All the chocolate, caramel and fun toppings of a whole apple, but served in easy-to-enjoy slices. My girls loved decorating these treats as much as they loved eating them.

And to be honest, even though they’re easy for kids, they’re easier for adults just the same! Plus, the slices are shareable. This format makes them ideal if you’re looking for simple Friendsgiving ideas or low-lift Thanksgiving desserts.

You’ll start by cutting 1/2-inch thick slices from a whole apple. I like to trim the curviest part first and leave it for a snack, while focusing on the broader part of the apple for the slices. You will also need to strategically work around the core and pick out any seeds before proceeding. From there, you can either insert a candy stick or simply use a bamboo skewer, as I did here.

For the chocolate coating, I prefer to use almond bark chocolate coating instead of traditional chocolate bars or chips. It melts more smoothly and sets quickly without the fussy tempering required for real chocolate.

Cut the apples lengthwise into 1/2-inch thick slices. Insert a stick or skewer into one end of each slice. Cover a baking sheet in parchment, and set aside.

In a microwave-safe bowl, heat the almond bark in 30-second intervals until melted, stirring after each interval.

Spoon the melted chocolate coating over the apple slices, and place them on the prepared baking sheet.

Decorate each chocolate apple slice as desired. Allow the chocolate coating to firm up and set at room temperature before enjoying.

I love serving these candy caramel apple slices on a stick because it makes them so easy to eat. My girls loved them because it’s like having giant, fancy lollipops. You can use either a candy stick (you might be able to find them in the baking section of grocery stores) or a bamboo skewer. Candy sticks might not be as readily available, but they are sturdier. Bamboo skewers are effortless to insert and easy to find, but they are a little flimsier, and you have to be careful not to poke yourself while eating the apple.

What candy combo would you make? Let us know in the comments below!

#6553. The Fall Winter 2026 Fashion Trends to Know and Shop Now

If recent seasons have been defined by understated dressing, the fall-winter 2026 trends mark a shift toward a more expressive approach to style. However, there’s still a piece of the cake for every aesthetic to cut into. Across the runways, designers embraced the art of contrast. By pairing clean, minimalist silhouettes with rich textures—and reimagining classic wardrobe staples with unexpected details like a peplum or a voluminous shape—they proved that practicality and personality can coexist. The result is a season that feels both wearable and exciting.

Leading the conversation this season are six standout trends that capture fashion’s evolving mood. The Updated Lady introduces a fresh take on suiting for the modern woman, complete with feminine touches and softened structures. (Take a look at Chanel, Balenciaga, and Jil Sander for fresh inspiration, for starters.) Elsewhere, collections at Khaite, Kallmeyer, and Conner Ives nodded to the golden age of the 1920s, incorporating elegant Art Deco touches throughout. An unexpected take on proportions has entered the chat, too, with Tory Burch and Celine reconfiguring preconceived notions of size and shape. Designers, from Prada to Loewe, leaned on the power of styling, too, showcasing how layering and a close attention to detail can transform a wardrobe. For a more alluring take on the season, Alaïa and Valentino celebrated the female form through body-hugging silhouettes and delicate sheer pieces. Meanwhile, Dries Van Noten and Erdem embraced the spirit of fall with down-to-earth palettes of green and brown, punctuated by dark floral patterns.

Discover a shoppable first look at the key fall winter 2026 fashion trends before they fully take over. Don’t forget to come back to this story for more.

Unlike past seasons, there wasn’t one definitive silhouette for tailoring this fall. Let’s start with suiting. Designers don’t want you to stay within the lines. Many jackets were shown with mismatched trousers and skirts; lapel linings were exposed; traditional collared shirts were left undone and wrinkled; collars were turned up and styled with one in and one out. Some blazers shrank; some went long and lean. Others were cropped, nipped in, or even made sculptural.

In autumn’s sea of black coats and navy sweaters, choose color. This season, designers made it simple, showing a slew of head-to-toe looks in vivid monochrome hues. Take your pick! The runways offered a spin around the contemporary color wheel with splashes of color-drenched leather bags and footwear. From knits to denim, dresses to outerwear, we can’t think of a reason not to try this kind of energetic dressing.

This isn’t your grandmother’s lace! On the fall runways, designers from Altuzarra and Colleen Allen to Bottega Veneta, Dior, and Gabriela Hearst embraced a more dramatic kind of romance, with cascading layers, frothy ruffles, and sheer, sweeping silhouettes. Get the look with a delicate lace blouse paired with a tiered black skirt, or go all in with a floor-length lace dress. The effect is romantic, but anything but prim.

Photos: Courtesy of Kallmeyer, Khaite, Rabanne, Chanel, and Loro Piana

Although F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel, The Great Gatsby, predates the height of the design style, its themes of 1920s luxury have permanently associated the story with the movement’s signature geometric patterns and overt opulence. From Khaite to Colleen Allen, designers embraced the era with richly detailed texture, glamorous shapes, fringe, gloves, and velvet. To quote the iconic host himself: “Can’t repeat the past? Why, of course, you can!” For 2026, the era returns with a modern, streamlined touch—ready for daily wear to elegant soirées.

Photos: Courtesy of Chanel, Stella McCartney, Givenchy, Jil Sander, and Chloé

The fall-winter 2026 runways showcased a sense of whimsy through bold proportions, featuring oversized designs, cropped styles, and exaggerated silhouettes. Cocoon-like tailoring, dramatic hemlines, and billowy pants and dresses create an expressive and eye-catching approach to fashion. This trend embraces a bit of drama (because that’s life!) while also maintaining a sense of balance. Unconventional silhouettes might feel daunting to incorporate into your daily lineup, so start with small touches. Destree’s jacquard blouse balances voluminous shoulders with a fitted waist that pairs easily with jeans, while Aflalo’s tapered white balloon pants feel airy and light—just add a layered knit and coat for transitional dressing.

Photos: Courtesy of Ferragamo, Loewe, Prada, Johanna Parv, The Row (middle)

Primarily inspired by the fall/winter 2026 Prada runway, the power of styling was a reminder that great style isn’t about owning more—it’s about seeing familiar pieces, like cardigans and tailored trousers, in a new light. Everyday wardrobe staples were transformed through unique pairings, layered basics, and unexpected accessories to create ensembles that demand a second glance. Styling, too, becomes a vessel for self-expression, allowing you to make each piece your own through personal touches and a careful attention to detail.

Photos: Courtesy of Dior, Chanel, Givenchy, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler, Kallmeyer

Current, confident, and sophisticated, the Updated Lady emerged as one of fall-winter 2026’s defining archetypes, with houses like Chanel, Givenchy, and Balenciaga reimagining power dressing through a contemporary lens. Rather than rigid corporate suiting, the season favored softened structures, explored through gently sloping waists, sculpted jackets, and rich textures that balance strength with ease. The modern woman is multifaceted and full of contradictions, balancing polish with her own distinct edge—shouldn’t her wardrobe follow suit?

Photos: Courtesy of Gucci, Gorunway.com, Khaite and Alaïa

Bodies, bodies, bodies! The fall 2026 runways were an homage to the female form. From the second-skin dresses at Alaïa—some of which actually walked in flesh-colored nude—to Khaite’s sheer layers and Valentino’s lingerie-inspired slips, little was left to the imagination. Translating the trend into your own fall rotation may seem far-fetched, but by embracing it piece by piece, you can achieve an alluring look without going full naked dressing. Imagine Jil Sander’s knit bustier top with a slim trouser, Gucci’s cut-out leggings grounded by a crisp white tee, or one of Saint Lauren’s lace mini dresses beneath a sharp tailored blazer. To bring it back to one of the season’s strongest show notes—and one we outlined above: It all comes down to the styling.

It’s not unusual for fall trends to find inspiration in the countryside—whether it’s heritage plaids, khaki barn jackets, or some kind of cozy knit variation. As grounding as the source material may be, this season’s expression is more elaborate than ever. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the floral prints peppered throughout the collections: they’re richer, deeper, and even moodier than in years’ past. Par for the course, intricate floral brocades appeared at Dries Van Noten on everything from outerwear to midiskirts. Simone Rocha and Erdem also showcased their fair share of flora and fauna, from draped dresses to blouses, proving that the look can move between moods and occasions.

#6551. In ‘Possible Love,’ Jeon Do-yeon Delivers the Year’s Most Shattering Performance. Can It Take Her to the Oscars?

In the nearly three decades since she made her big-screen debut in 1997’s The Contact, Jeon Do-yeon has earned a richly deserved reputation in South Korea—and far beyond it—as the kind of actor who inhabits her characters so fully that it ceases to feel like acting at all. (International audiences likely know her best for 2007’s Secret Sunshine, a wrenching portrait of a grieving mother that made her the first Korean performer to win an acting prize at the Cannes Film Festival.)

Critics often reach for the word “fearless” to describe her, but when we speak via Zoom at the tail end of a marathon press day in Seoul, Jeon waves that notion away.

“I’m always scared, and I’m full of fear, especially in front of the camera,” she says, with a laugh. “I’ve been working as an actor for quite some time, but it’s an ongoing process.” In fact, it’s important to her that she never gets too comfortable. “I actually enjoy having that fear and anxiety, and trying my best to work through it, because sometimes something completely new comes out of that struggle.”

That willingness to sit in discomfort is vividly, devastatingly evident in Possible Love, out now on Netflix after a theatrical run in October—and recently selected as South Korea’s official submission for the 2027 Academy Awards. The film marks the long-awaited return of legendary auteur Lee Chang-dong (arguably best known for the hypnotic 2018 masterpiece Burning, which became the first Korean movie ever shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar and topped critics’ year-end lists across the West) after an eight-year hiatus, and a reunion for Jeon and Lee nearly 20 years after Secret Sunshine.

Constructed with Lee’s signature novelistic sweep, Possible Love centers on the complicated dynamic between two married couples from starkly different strata of contemporary Korean society. Jeon stars as Mi-ok, a pragmatic mask-factory worker living quietly with her young son and her husband, Ho-seok (played by her frequent screen partner Sul Kyung-gu). Years after a mass factory layoff and a violently suppressed labor strike, Ho-seok remains haunted by the trauma. When the funeral of a former co-worker brings them into the orbit of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, best known as the rich mom in Parasite), an intellectual documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off laborers, and her wealthy, enigmatic husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), Mi-ok agrees to let Ye-ji film their daily lives. Yet what begins as a study of liberal empathy—and a moving portrait of across-the-divide solidarity—gradually warps into something far more strange and ambiguous, exploring the fault lines of privilege, hidden desire, and voyeurism.

Oscar buzz has swirled around her performance—a stunning and powerfully subtle tightrope walk of stoicism and simmering longing—since the film premiered at the Venice Film Festival in September, but Jeon remains pragmatic about what all this fanfare actually means. “When I won the award at Cannes 20 years ago, I remember thinking, Is this going to change my life? Probably not. Am I going to change as an actor because I have a Cannes award?” she reflects. “I’m very happy that we’re competing at the Oscars, and it’s wonderful that people are talking about the film, but I don’t think it will change me or the way I perform in any way.”

Below, Jeon discusses her on-screen reunion with Sul Kyung-gu, the unlikely magic fostered by Lee Chang-dong’s aversion to having his actors rehearse, and how a story of trauma and class tension deeply rooted in Korean society found universal resonance.

Vogue: Now that Possible Love is streaming on Netflix and reaching a massive global audience, how are you feeling? Have you been hearing much feedback?

Jeon Do-yeon: I watched the movie once again as soon as it was on Netflix. I think Possible Love is a type of movie that leaves a different afterglow for different people, and people can analyze it differently and interpret it in endless ways. Now that it’s on Netflix, I feel like people are finding their own ways to think about the movie—it leaves a lot of food for thought. I’m very proud that people are talking a lot about it.

To go back to the beginning, you obviously have a deep history with director Lee Chang-dong. How did he first approach you about Possible Love? I believe this idea had been gestating for almost a decade.

I do know that Director Lee worked on this project for quite a long time—he had it in his mind for more than 10 years. Ten years ago, he wanted to talk about this worker and his wife, the couple who had been laid off. Sometimes that story diverged into different paths, and sometimes they were scrapped; I know there were a lot of different versions along the way. When I knew that he finally had a script, I really wanted to know what it was about. I was waiting for that script. [Laughs.]

Given how layered the story is, what struck you most when you finally read it? What drew you to Mi-ok?

When I first read the script, I could feel the 10 years’ worth of thought and effort that Director Lee put into it. I was very touched reading it, and I was like, “Of course this is a Chang-dong film. It is this good.” And then I thought about what I could relate to about my character, Mi-ok. Of all the traits that she has, I think she holds this anxiety, and that anxiety stems from her wish to protect certain things. Although Mi-ok may seem a little bit fragile or weak from the outside, I think she’s a very strong woman inside, so that is something that I took note of.

Zo In-sung as Sang-woo, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, and director Lee Chang-dong on the set of Possible Love.

One of the aspects of your performance I found most striking is the physicality—the way Mi-ok holds herself is such an important part of how her story is told. Did you develop that beforehand, or did you find it on set?

If I hadn’t worked with Director Lee before, then I would have spent a lot of time trying to learn more about this character and to deeply understand her. But I know how he works, and he always stresses emptying my mind as an actor. He wants me not to express, but to feel the character. The preparation process for me was mostly about making sure that I get very accustomed to the lines that my character speaks, so it really feels like it’s me speaking, but it’s actually Mi-ok speaking through me.

You’ve worked with Sul Kyung-gu more than any other actor in your career, I believe. So much of the film relies on the subtleties of that relationship—did your real-life friendship and trust help?

I think I really know him well in real life, and as an actor as well. But while we were working on this project, and as he transformed into the character of Ho-seok, I discovered new facets of him. There’s always a new side of him that would surprise me, so I’m still looking forward to working with him on another project so I can discover yet another new side of him. We have this friendship and trust that we’ve built over the years, and I’m pretty sure that they helped. When you’re trying to express the chemistry of a very long relationship of a married couple, sometimes you have to make efforts to show that aspect. But we didn’t have to try too hard because we already had that trust built between us. If we do look like a real married couple in the movie, I think it’s partly thanks to that.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok.

At the opposite end of the spectrum, this was your first time working with Cho Yeo-jeong. The dynamic between Mi-ok and Ye-ji walks a very delicate line between sisterhood and something more transactional. Did the two of you discuss that, or did you prefer to discover it in the room?

We actually didn’t talk about our characters before going into production. When you work with Director Lee, he’s sort of against the actors having too many biases or prejudices or information about characters before going into the shoot, because he believes something very novel and fresh can come out when it’s your first time being in that scene, when it’s your first time talking. I didn’t want to jinx that by speaking with her about our characters beforehand. In the beginning, my character, Mi-ok, believes that if Ye-ji films us, then that is a way of protecting my family—a way of finding hope. But as they get closer, she realizes that there is a gap between the two people, herself and Ye-ji, and the wall grows higher and higher as they get closer.

Director Lee is known for his naturalism. Did that mean doing dozens of takes until you lost the sense that you’re acting? Did scenes ever head in unexpected directions based on how you were all interacting?

Director Lee is not actually the type who shoots a lot of takes, because he doesn’t really tell us exactly what it is that he wants from a scene. What he tries to do instead is to look into the chemistry and the conversation between the actors and try to find something new from it. Instead of Director Lee saying, “Okay, let’s do the lines,” he would just say, “Why don’t we talk? Let’s talk.” He likes everything very lively and raw, so that’s how we did it, and he didn’t want us to have a lot of rehearsals. And regarding whether the direction of a scene actually changed after working—it didn’t happen, because there was no fixed direction in the beginning.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji.

Korean cinema has obviously exploded in popularity globally over the past decade, and Possible Love is getting a huge amount of international attention. How do you view this global wave? Do you think much about reaching Western audiences?

I don’t have plans on “going global” or anything as an actor! But I do hope that Korean content and Korean cinema will be beloved around the globe going forward as well. It’s just such a joy to be able to share different stories and different emotions with people that speak different languages and have different cultures. It’s such a good opportunity for us to transcend borders, transcend language. I hope more of those opportunities will come.

Possible Love is rooted in a very specific Korean tragedy, yet the hollowing out of industrial working-class communities is something people recognize all over the world. Did you worry at all during filming about whether such a locally specific story would translate, especially on a global platform like Netflix?

When we were filming, we actually did think about how this is a very Korea-specific sort of incident. Would people around the world be able to resonate with this story? Particularly because there is no dramatic event that happens throughout the movie; it’s just about the four people and their emotions, and that’s what really brings a narrative towards the end. We were a little bit worried. But I actually realized after screening overseas that the issue of laid-off workers is not something that’s specific to Korea—it’s happening all around the world, and it is still happening in some parts of the world. I could feel that a lot of people who are not Korean, who don’t live in Korea, are resonating with the themes and the emotions that are captured in the movie. And the moon at the very end of the movie? Anybody in any part of the world can see the moon. That’s something that’s very universal.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6549. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6548. A Major Liquor Brand Is Making A Comeback After Filing For Bankruptcy

And its comeback comes with a few more spirits to its roster.

Earlier this year, college kids everywhere had reason to worry about losing Stoli Vodka. Back in January, creditors were pushing for the liquidation of Stoli Group's U.S. operations, putting both Stoli Vodka and Kentucky Owl bourbon at risk. Now, however, the company's future in the States is looking a whole lot brighter.

According to the company, it has completed its restructuring after filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2024. If the case had shifted to Chapter 7, a court-appointed trustee could have taken control of the affected U.S. operations and overseen their liquidation. But Stoli Group has since reached a settlement with creditors of Stoli Group (USA), allowing it to resume supplying products to the American market.

In a press release, Stoli says it already has inventory in a U.S. customs warehouse and is working with longtime distribution partners to get products into participating markets.

In addition to Stoli Vodka and elit Vodka, Stoli Group is expanding its lineup of products in the States with Moskovskaya Vodka, Rooster Rojo and KAH tequilas, and The Irishman and Writers' Tears Irish whiskeys. Bayou Rum is also getting updates to the rum itself, its packaging, and pricing, with U.S. production of flavored Stoli vodkas and Stoli Ginger Beer, a nonalcoholic mixer, also to come.

"The U.S. has always been an important market for Stoli, and we're eager to share that Stoli is back and better than ever," said Marina Troyanovskaya, chief commercial officer of Stoli Group. "Our products are already here, we have longstanding partners who know our brands, and we're focused on reconnecting with consumers across the country."
