Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6536. 25 Festive Thanksgiving Cocktails To Get The Party Started

You could go the usual route and pair your Thanksgiving feast with a classic bottle of red wine. Or, you could mix things up with one of these festive cocktails that were made for the holiday. These fall cocktails are FAR more fun than a plain ol' bottle of wine, and will keep the good times going long after the turkey has been carved and the pie has been served.

The holidays are the perfect time to brush up on your home bartending skills. We love mixing up a signature cocktail to pair with our Thanksgiving dinner, as it adds that certain special something to the table. Thankfully, the most classic cocktails also happen to be some of the simplest, too. Looking for something with a little more of a spin for the holiday? Try our cranberry Hugo spritz, spiced apple Paloma, or pumpkin margaritas for festive takes on the classics.

Pro tip: These fall cocktails taste even better with our favorite Thanksgiving apps or a slice of pumpkin or apple pie. Crowd still thirsty? For more festive drinks, try our amazing Thanksgiving punch ideas that make hosting easier than ever.

Cider and ginger beer might seem like a weird pairing, but with fresh fruit and cinnamon (plus bubbly!), we promise you it more than works. For a small but just as rowdy brunch, make our caramel apple mimosas instead.

A classic Hugo spritz is decidedly a summer cocktail, but if you’re looking for an excuse to pop a bottle of Prosecco in colder weather, look no further than this cranberry Hugo spritz.

Your chai latte just got a Saturday night makeover. With vodka, Kahlúa, fresh espresso, and a generous pour of chai syrup, this is the kind of drink that makes people ask for the recipe before they've even finished the glass.

Sangria might make you think of warm summer nights and tropical fruits, but this apple-based cocktail will have you ready for fall. Here, we went for a white wine sangria, rounded out with spicy ginger beer and sweet apple cider.

Our cranberry Collins is herbaceous, tangy, and effervescent, making it the ideal companion to turkey and all your favorite sides. This refreshing cocktail blends crisp gin, zesty lemon, tart cranberry juice, and aromatic thyme, topped with bubbly club soda for a lively finish.

Think Aperol spritz, but whereas that one is firmly a summer sipper, this spritz has a darker, more savory vibe that makes it great for enjoying with or after dinner any time of year.

Shaken and poured into a chilled glass, dessert cocktails are the ultimate end-of-the-night treat, especially when they include mocha and bourbon. This boozy Turkeytini has all you need to complete your Thanksgiving feast with the decadent blend of creamy Baileys Irish cream, chocolate liqueur, Kahlúa, and bourbon.

This Thanksgiving, we’re trading the sour-sweet Paloma's summery pink shade for a cozy, fireside glow. Equal parts bright, spiced, and sparkling, it’s the perfect bridge between cozy sweater moments and champagne-worthy celebrations.

Your pumpkin spice latte, now all grown up! Whether you just want a fun nightcap or want to have a signature cocktail at Thanksgiving, these white Russians are sure to be a crowd-pleaser.

The holidays usually usher in seasonal cocktails with cozy spices to stay warm in the winter, but we think bright, refreshing beverages should be enjoyed all year long. If you love sipping on margaritas and palomas but want a more festive recipe to enjoy during the holiday season, meet the cranberry paloma..

This cocktail is perfect for when you've been cooking inside all day, and can't decide whether to grab a glass of red or white—reach for the apple cider and tequila instead! The hot honey here is the perfect sweet with a little heat, and Calvados adds hints of caramel apple and kettle corn.

While a glass of Lambrusco is always good served on its own, it’s also a fantastic starting point for a cocktail. The smoky mezcal, bright orange citrus, and spice from the ginger beer here tie together beautifully, giving you a zingy, sweet-ish, refreshing, and original cocktail.

The combination of pumpkin pie filling, pumpkin spice syrup (optional; see below for method), and reposado tequila creates a beautiful autumnal blend. The aged tequila adds a rich brown sugar flavor that mixes perfectly with the pumpkin ingredients, while the bright acidity from the lime balances the cocktail and provides that classic margarita tang.

To make a truly fall version of the hot toddy, we needed to make an apple cider version. (Pumpkin spice, wait your turn. 😉)

We kicked a classic chai latte up a notch to create this spiked pumpkin version—in it, freshly steeped chai and a shot of whiskey get blended with milk, pumpkin puree, and maple syrup, then topped with whipped cream. It’s the perfect after-dinner drink for a chilly Thanksgiving.

Move over, hot toddy—there's a new hot drink in town, and the name is fireside negroni. We dressed up the tried and true Negroni with Earl Grey tea and a touch of maple syrup. As the season transitions and the days get shorter, we look to hot cocktails like this one to keep the chill out of our bones.

Cranberry adds a festive, blood-red twist to your favorite cocktail, the Aperol spritz. If you don't want it to be too sweet, you can swap the cranberry juice cocktail for 100% cranberry juice.

Super-excited for fall and all the fun fall activities that come with it—pumpkin carving, Thanksgiving, apple picking? These cocktails are for you! They're the best of summery margaritas, plus spicy, seasonal apple cider.

The last three months of the year mean it's time to party, and what better way to say party in a cocktail than punch? This kalimoxto-inspired sangria upgrade is literally a little bit of this, a little bit of that with a top off of everyone's favorite soda—an ice cold Coca-Cola.

In this fall rendition of everyone's favorite summer spritz, we included a woodsy rosemary sprig and fig syrup to welcome fall’s rich earthy flavors and make the easiest large format cocktail that will impress everyone at your holiday table. Thanksgiving’s aperitivo hour just got a delicious upgrade.

#6533. Hidden in the Viral Last Ditch Debacle: How to Keep Lesbian Bars Alive

By September of this year, Jackie Matellian had spent months living in her truck while working several jobs to keep Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, open. She was the last remaining original founder, and the bar was in deep financial trouble. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, workers had gone unpaid, Matellian was carrying a $50,000 start-up loan, and the landlord wanted $3,900 in overdue rent.

Last Ditch had been built to do things most bars don’t even attempt. It welcomed lesbians, transsexuals, and other queer people who couldn’t afford the cover, offered a free store with food, clothing and harm-reduction supplies, and required KN95 masks or better. For immunocompromised patrons, those precautions made it possible to have a night out without gambling with their health. The bar’s radical inclusiveness was part of why people cared about it—and part of what its owners were struggling to finance it.

Desperate for cash, the bar’s management announced a policy shift with a cheery Instagram post: Saturday nights would become mask-optional. The gamble backfired. By treating accessibility as negotiable, the bar alienated immunocompromised regulars without attracting enough new customers to pay the rent. Follow-up stumbles culminated in a marathon three-and-a-half-hour community meeting that collapsed without a resolution. Rather than saving the venue, the policy pivot left Last Ditch with the worst of both worlds: fractured community trust and an unresolved financial crisis.

The drama became national entertainment, right up until October 26, when Last Ditch announced its soft closure.

The spectators moved on, but one issue remains: expecting one struggling lesbian bar to compensate for the failures of an entire social infrastructure is absurd. The irony is that Western Massachusetts built the blueprint for combating exactly this.

Women in the area have been finding ways to share the costs of lesbian social life for decades. UMass Amherst documents more than 400 lesbian and feminist groups active in the region between 1968 and 1978. Northampton had the Common Womon Club, Lesbian Gardens, Womonfyre Books, and the Nutcracker’s Suite self-defense dojo. These were places women built to make their social lives and organizing possible outside institutions that routinely excluded them.

In 1976, the women behind Common Womon pooled money to buy property through Ceres Inc., the nonprofit they’d formed, then financed renovations with help from donations and a loan. The adjacent storefront provided rental income and housed the Nutcracker’s Suite, then Womonfyre Books, so control of the property also gave the women a way to make room for other projects and help pay for the place they shared. Common Womon also collected sliding-scale membership dues, while the Valley Women’s History Collaborative lists benefits for the Common Womon Club that helped keep it going.

The womon-spelling and the names are fun to inherit; I also want us to inherit the ability to put actual premises under our control. For Last Ditch, that begins with finding out whether a new set of owners can remain in the building on terms the business can afford.

Matellian had already told the Globe she planned to turn the bar into a cooperative. For that to relieve the pressure on her, new members would need to take responsibility for work she’d been doing and agree on how the existing debt would be handled. But calling it a cooperative wouldn’t do much for Matellian if she was still the person everyone called whenever something went wrong. Sharing authority has to include sharing responsibility for the work, with limits on what any one person is expected to carry.

Sharing ownership would give people more power over decisions and occasions to disagree about them. Common Womon closed in 1982, while Womonfyre lasted until 1989. Womonfyre faced harassment and threats from outside the lesbian community as well as conflicts over sexual politics and what the shop should sell. Its archive preserves those disputes alongside bank statements and instructions for running the store.

A cooperative at Last Ditch would need procedures for making decisions in tandem with conflict resolution. Which is why I like that the Womonfyre archive makes room for instructions on running the shop alongside political disputes. A disagreement over how to run a bar doesn’t become abuse because people are arguing. Treating every conflict as a verdict on someone’s character makes it harder to agree on a change, because the argument can continue long after the conduct has stopped or the policy has been reversed.

Making that possible at Last Ditch requires paid training and a written account of all this work. A cooperative whose members can debate the mission for four hours but can’t cover a shift or pay its debt will end up crushing the same woman behind the bar.

If Last Ditch is to survive, its next incarnation must trade endless character trials for operational infrastructure: shared labor, transparent books, and creative financing strategies.

If one thing the Globe’s reporting revealed, it is that one commercial bar bearing the weight of an entire community’s social safety crushes everyone under impossible expectations. Instead, we must look for ways to anchor the politics in practical economics, share the burden, and build a room strong enough to hold the argument without tearing down the house.

Anyone asking the community to save Last Ditch needs to be prepared to share control of what survives.

#6530. Chick-fil-A Is Saying Goodbye To Its Chicken & Waffles—But There’s A Twist

The waffles aren’t going down without a fight.

If you’ve been loving Chick-fil-A’s new Chicken & Waffles menu (me, I have), you might want to make another breakfast run before it’s too late. The chain’s limited-time lineup is officially on its way out, but a few lucky cities are getting an expanded version with even more options.

Chick-fil-A's nationwide Chicken & Waffles offerings are scheduled to disappear after November 14, while supplies last. But starting November 16, select restaurants in Tampa, FL; Chicago; and Raleigh, NC, will test five different waffle breakfast sandwiches.

The extended menu includes the Chicken & Waffles Breakfast Sandwich, which customers can order with Chick-fil-A’s Original, Spicy, or Grilled chicken fillet. So whether you're looking for something crispy, a little heat, or a grilled option, there’s a version for you.

But the real excitement comes from the four additional sandwiches being tested.

The new Chicken, Egg & Cheese Waffle Sandwich combines chicken with a classic breakfast pairing, while the Bacon, Egg & Cheese Waffle Sandwich swaps the usual breakfast bread for waffles. There’s also a Sausage, Egg & Cheese Waffle Sandwich, and for anyone who wants a little bit of everything, a Grilled Chicken, Bacon, Egg & Cheese Waffle Sandwich.

According to Chick-fil-A, the expanded test follows a positive response to its Chicken & Waffles menu this fall.

The expanded breakfast menu will be available at participating restaurants in Tampa, Chicago, and Raleigh from opening until 10:30 a.m., while supplies last. Customers can check the Chick-fil-A app to see whether their local restaurant is participating.

As for the rest of us, we have until November 14 to enjoy the nationwide Chicken & Waffles lineup before it disappears.

Here’s hoping the test goes well, because I’d happily trade my usual breakfast sandwich bun for a couple of waffles.

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6527. Regal Cinemas May Switch From Pepsi To Coca-Cola Next Year, Insiders Reveal

Coke or Pepsi? These days, we don’t have much choice.

Rumors are swirling that Regal Cinemas plans to end its partnership with Pepsi and start serving Coca-Cola products at theaters nationwide starting next year. The chain hasn’t publicly announced the switch, but one Regal employee on Reddit appeared to confirm that it’s not just hearsay.

“As a current employee, I can confirm this,” they wrote. “We had some Coke reps visit our location and take photos and see our soda layouts in the concessions area.”

Regal has bounced between the two beverage companies over the years. The movie theater chain served Pepsi products from its founding until 2002, when it pivoted to an 18-year exclusive contract with Coca-Cola. Regal reverted to Pepsi products in 2020 and called the partnership “an epic love story destined for the big screen.” Now, it seems like there’s no love lost.

Moviegoers are largely excited by this development. “Oh this is absolutely the best news possible!! It's literally been the singular downside to becoming such a Regal goer the past few years,” one X user wrote. Another added, “I am a Pepsi enjoyer, but if this is what it takes to get a cola-flavored Icee back in my Regal then I am all for it.”

If true, Regal would join a growing list of chains dropping Pepsi as its beverage partner. Last summer, Costco ended its 12-year contract to start serving Coca-Cola in its food courts. And, just last month, KFC announced that it, too, would start serving Coca-Cola products.

Anybody who keeps tabs on the drink company is probably unsurprised. PepsiCo has shuttered two bottling plants in Maryland and Tennessee since September. In a third-quarter earnings call last month, CEO Ramon Laguarta said that the company isn’t “competing well in soft drinks” and that he doesn’t “feel good” about how its beverage business is performing.

The company is also planning price hikes across its food and beverage portfolio to compensate for the rising costs of aluminum and diesel. With increasing prices and shrinking distribution, it appears serving Pepsi is losing its luster for some foodservice chains. Whether or not it stops with Regal remains to be seen.

#6525. The Mysterious Fridge Hacks Hitting Grocery Stores

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the Cheesecake Factory culture war.

Death, taxes, and Martha Stewart doing something weird online every six to eight weeks: These are the constants in our ever-chaotic lives. This round involved a quickly deleted Instagram post showing Stewart apparently dressed as a homeless person—she was holding a clipboard (?) with a message in marker that read “I am hungry help me!!”

She released a series of statements apologizing for the gaffe, and at one point seemed to blame Today show host Craig Melvin, who, she said, spilled chocolate on the sweater she’d planned on wearing to a costume party later that night, forcing her to improvise a new costume on the fly.

But enough of Martha! We have more important things to worry about.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the mysterious refrigeration system hacks plaguing Europe, DC's newly minted foie gras ban, the GLP-1 gap relationship, and a democratic victory is celebrated at a Whataburger, naturally.

Dozens of supermarkets across seven countries were the victims of hacking that took control of their refrigeration systems this week. The hackers shifted grocery freezers into defrost mode, the freezers began blowing hot air onto the frozen food, and, in some, temperatures rose to 122 degrees. Needless to say a lot of food was deemed spoiled and had to be thrown out.

Three weeks ago, similar attacks hit grocery stores in France. It was the same story: defrost mode, hot air, lots of wasted food and money. Officials are investigating who may be responsible, but so far the culprits and their motives remain a mystery. The BBC reports that experts believe hackers in Russia or Iran—or simply teenagers playing a prank—could be responsible.

Could something like this happen in the US? Well, it sort of already has. In August six military bases across the country reported some odd refrigeration malfunctions—the same kind we’ve been seeing in Europe. The Pentagon is investigating the incident as a suspected hack, but that’s about as much information as we can glean.

The FBI on Thursday issued a warning about “malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world.”

As Democrats celebrated a resounding wave of victories in this week’s midterm elections, so too did duck and goose lovers. Washington, DC, voted to approve a ballot measure banning the sale and production of foie gras. It was a controversial issue in the area, as I covered in last week’s Open Tab video, which saw big name chefs come forward to defend the making, selling, and eating of foie gras. The discourse got heated, topical Halloween costumes abounded.

The ban will go into effect July 1, 2027, so foie-heads have some time to get their fill. But it’s not that simple. A New York foie gras company has said it will take legal action against the ban, calling it “unconstitutional on several grounds." To put the ban in effect would face further logistical barriers too. DC’s chief financial officer has estimated it would cost more than $300,000 over four fiscal years to implement it—money that’s not currently allocated in the budget.

Despite the upcoming ban, Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s who was one of the ban’s most vocal opponents, has said he’ll continue serving foie gras in his restaurants. “I will still be serving it for another decade,” he told the Washington Post.

What happens when one partner gets on a GLP-1 and the other partner doesn’t? We know that GLP-1’s can shift your sex drive, and that they can have an effect on your mental health, but often, it seems, there’s anecdotal evidence that they can have a profound effect on your relationships. A report in the Washington Post details how, for some couples, starting a GLP-1 can disrupt a couple's routines and equilibrium—deciding on a date night restaurant, for instance—which can create divisions. There simply isn’t enough data to measure how GLP-1’s might be linked to divorce rates, but some experts point to statistics attached to bariatric surgeries, another weight loss intervention, which found that married couples are twice as likely to get divorced after getting the procedure.

Midterm elections in the US brought a number of historic firsts, including the first Muslim senator (Michigan), the first openly gay man senator (New Hampshire), and the first Black woman governor (Georgia). Notably, voters managed to flip Texas, turning the state blue for the first time in decades.

How did Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa celebrate their wins? At a Whataburger. It’s a surprisingly poignant statement about the affordability politics that was foundational to many Democratic wins this election cycle. Read on to learn more.

#6524. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

#6523. We Tried 8 Store-Bought Mashed Potatoes & These Are Worth Bringing To Thanksgiving

Supermarket shortcuts that (almost) taste homemade.

Making a full holiday menu can be a monumental task, so you can—and should—outsource some of the cooking. The Thanksgiving dishes that you can reliably buy from the supermarket are the ones that are almost impossible to screw up. Case in point: mashed potatoes.

The essential side requires peeling pounds of potatoes, meticulous mashing, and taking up stove space (a precious commodity on Turkey Day). But at its core, the recipe is as simple as it gets. So if you want to save time and energy this year, store-bought spuds are a shortcut absolutely worth taking.

To help you decide which one to add to your Thanksgiving menu, we tasted eight varieties of mashed potatoes to identify the best of the best. We only considered refrigerated versions that are ready to heat and eat (no instant potatoes, thanks!). Here’s the verdict from our blind taste test.

Wegmans offers a few varieties of mashed potatoes, but the classic Whipped recipe is our favorite. It also has the shortest ingredient list: just potatoes, milk, butter, salt, and a small amount of natural food preservative. That simplicity translates to a product that tastes close to homemade.

Our editors appreciate the richness, real potato flavor, and chunks that add a rustic texture. They’re well-seasoned and can be eaten on their own, while still basic enough to pair with the rest of your Thanksgiving plate. These were the potatoes News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas tried first, and she knew after one bite they’d be her favorite. (Spoiler alert: they were.)

Another top contender comes from Sam’s Club with its private-label Yukon Gold mash. The ingredients start similarly to Wegmans', with potatoes, milk, and butter, though the Sam's Club version also includes black pepper and natural flavoring. But notable differences show up when you taste them side by side.

The Member’s Mark mash puts butter front and center and is seasoned a bit more generously than our overall winner. The richness is dialed up to 11. While some of us enjoyed it, a few found the butter to be too overpowering. But if you’re a butter lover, you won’t be disappointed by this Sam’s Club recipe.

Mashed potatoes are a bit like peanut butter: Some like it chunky, while others prefer creamy. If you fall in the latter camp, the Traditional Mashed Potatoes from Simply Potatoes is your best bet. The brand is widely available at major retailers and is distributed by Bob Evans Farms (note that the other mashed potatoes bearing his name did not make this list). This recipe includes margarine and a few extra preservatives, but the main ingredients are still potatoes, milk, and butter.

Our editors agree that the mash from Simply Potatoes has “great potato flavor” and a silky-smooth texture. It’s looser than our other top picks, with a finish closer to a French pommes purée than a hearty mash. This is the brand to buy if you want to avoid chunky mashed potatoes this Thanksgiving.

How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

Carr, C., Cen, R., McCandliss, S., Ford, J., Saldana-Lopez, A., Scarlata, C., Huberty, M. S., Jaskot, A., Flury, S., Oey, M. S., Amorín, R. O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

#6521. Chatpata Potato Chip Tower

Cookbook author Rachel Gurjar doesn’t usually jump on food trends, but the potato chip tower called to her. “Chips are already great as is, but I knew a version inspired by chana chor—a fiery street snack made from flattened, fried black chickpeas tossed with onions, chiles, lemon, and chaat masala—would kick it up a notch,” she writes in her debut title, East to East. Chatpata is a Hindi word that means salty, sour, spicy, and sweet at the same time, and this chatpata potato chip tower absolutely lives up to its name. While you can use any potato chips you like—or even substitute tortilla chips, pita chips, or fried pita bread—Gurjar recommends thick kettle-cooked chips, as they stay crispy longer.

#6520. 53 Healthy Thanksgiving Recipes to Brighten Up the Table

What makes a healthy Thanksgiving recipe? To us, it’s less about cutting out butter or skipping pie and more about bringing balance to the table. Crisp, bitter greens make creamy mashed potatoes taste even better. Tart cranberries cut through rich turkey gravy. Beans, whole grains, and plenty of colorful vegetables bring flavor, texture, and variety to a meal that can otherwise skew decidedly beige.

These healthy Thanksgiving recipes cover the entire feast, from crunchy salads and make-ahead appetizers to satisfying plant-forward mains and festive desserts. Some offer more fiber or protein; others give seasonal produce a starring role. What they have in common is that every one is delicious. You’ll also find plenty of vegan, gluten-free, and dairy-free options too. Because there’s room for everyone—and everything—at the Thanksgiving table.

Deep purple cabbage, bitter radicchio, juicy citrus, and ruby-red pomegranate seeds make a strong case for putting salad front and center. Give the cabbage a good massage to soften it without sacrificing its crunch.

“In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake,” writes Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser. Here, thinly sliced pears get a shower of honey-roasted seeds and shaved cheese.

Instead of tender greens that might wilt before everyone sits down, consider a fennel salad that stays crunchy for hours. Walnuts, Parmesan, croutons, and lemon give it plenty of flavor and texture.

Who says salad has to be cold? Caramelized cauliflower, warm feta, crunchy pistachios, and sticky dates meet peppery arugula and a tangy vinaigrette. Hearty enough to satisfy, with plenty of greens to keep things fresh.

Bitter radicchio meets sweet apple and mustardy croutons in this hearty autumn salad. Tossing the apple slices with cider vinegar helps keep them from browning before the feast begins.

A Thanksgiving salad should be sturdy enough to hold its own on the buffet table. This one only gets better after it’s dressed, as the kale softens and the nutty pecan vinaigrette works its way into the leaves.

Cranberry sauce isn’t just for turkey. A tart dressing made with the canned stuff brings holiday spirit to bitter greens, sweetened pecans, and Manchego cheese. Consider it a little insurance against salad fatigue.

Warm spices and sweet carrots give this hearty lentil salad plenty of character. The legumes add plant-based protein and fiber, making it a substantial addition to a vegetarian Thanksgiving spread.

Panzanella isn’t just for summer. Swap ripe tomatoes for juicy oranges, add bitter chicories and shaved fennel, and toss everything with toasted pumpernickel croutons and a balsamic-Dijon vinaigrette.

Roasted carrots, chickpeas, almonds, and smoked paprika blend into a vibrant dip with a little protein and plenty of personality. Make it up to a week ahead, then serve with seeded crackers, crudités, or good bread.

Another excellent addition to the crudité platter. Hazelnuts bring out the earthy sweetness of beets, while garlic and lemon keep everything lively. Like the carrot dip above, this one can be made a week ahead.

A jar of olives, a block of feta, and some garlicky olive oil: That’s nearly all you need for this bright, briny appetizer. Have some crusty bread handy for the flavorful oil left in the bowl.

Yuzu kosho gives these deviled eggs a jolt of citrusy heat, while pickled shallots, fresh herbs, and thinly sliced radishes bring brightness and crunch. Arrange them on shiso leaves for an especially striking holiday appetizer.

A bowl of party nuts is never a bad idea, particularly when they’re seasoned with chile powder, fried curry leaves, and crispy onions. Set these out while the turkey finishes roasting.

A tangy, Parmesan-rich dressing clings to crisp-tender green beans, with pickled shallots bringing a sharp little kick. All the satisfaction of a proper Thanksgiving side, without the casserole dish.

Crispy onions are the crown on this roasted squash side; pomegranate seeds are the jewels. Add fresh herbs and a swoop of lemony yogurt, and you’ve got a dish worthy of the center of the table.

These collards aren’t cooked into submission. Simmered until just tender, they stay pleasantly substantial beneath a sharp mustard vinaigrette. Tarragon and sweet-salty walnuts finish this fresh take on a holiday greens side.

When the oven is too crowded for green bean casserole, make this stovetop alternative. Browned mushrooms, crisp-tender green beans, butter, and frizzled shallots deliver plenty of familiar holiday flavor.

One BA reader calls this their signature Thanksgiving sprouts recipe. Separating the individual leaves takes patience, but the payoff is worth it: tender-crisp greens with lots of caramelized edges.

Toss sprouts with spicy, nutty gochujang brown butter. Or, for something simpler, go for classic roasted brussels sprouts.

Coconut milk gives this bubbling, breadcrumb-topped vegan gratin its creamy consistency without any dairy. A little lemon zest and nutmeg round things out.

White miso gives these glazed carrots a deep savoriness, while scallion gremolata adds freshness. You can cook the carrots a day ahead and loosen the glaze with a splash of water when reheating.

Maple syrup plays up carrots’ natural sweetness, while a pinch of chile flakes keeps the glaze from going full candy. This is a classic Thanksgiving side with just enough heat to keep things interesting.

Or skip cooking the carrots altogether. Shave them into thin ribbons, let salt soften them slightly, then toss with sticky dates and an orange vinaigrette. Sweet, tart, crunchy, and fresh.

Blanch, smash, and dress the beans up to 12 hours ahead so they can soak up the lemony sumac vinaigrette. Finish with Asian pear, parsley, and crunchy pumpkin seeds just before serving.

Silken tofu gives this steakhouse classic its creamy texture without dairy. Aromatics add savory depth, making it a satisfying side to serve alongside turkey, stuffing, and potatoes.

Bitter greens, tangy heat, and salty crunch are especially welcome among Thanksgiving’s softer sides. Toss tender broccoli rabe with garlicky onions and pickled cherry peppers, then shower the lot with crisp Pecorino breadcrumbs.

The French bistro classic gets a holiday-friendly update: Cut the leeks into rounds rather than long stalks, making them easier to serve to a crowd. A sharp vinaigrette, toasted walnuts, and fresh tarragon finish the dish.

Steamed broccolini gets a salty-sweet dressing of tahini, miso, soy sauce, and mirin, then a scattering of lemon and sesame seeds. Make the sauce a day ahead to take one more task off your Thanksgiving list.

Sweet roasted beets meet tart grapefruit, sharp shallots, and sizzling rosemary. The colors alone could wake up a Thanksgiving spread. Plus, you can roast and peel the beets up to two days ahead.

Inspired by Cantonese steamed fish, this squash side gets a generous pouf of frizzled scallions. Ginger and chile bring the heat, turning a humble vegetable into something special.

Bharta is a Bangladeshi preparation of seasoned meat or mashed vegetables. This roasted squash version gets its punch from mustard oil, chiles, spices, and fresh cilantro.

Raw cranberries keep their tart snap in this bright relish, while toasted walnuts, mustard seeds, Fresno chile, and a little maple syrup bring crunch, heat, and sweetness. Make it up to four days ahead.

A quick parboil and a vigorous shake rough up the surfaces of these potatoes, helping them develop exceptionally crunchy crusts in the oven. The fluffy centers are practically made for soaking up gravy.

Baking potatoes instead of boiling them concentrates their flavor, while roasted garlic adds savory depth. With just six tablespoons of butter for four pounds of potatoes, this creamy mash is a little less indulgent than many holiday versions.

Steaming sweet potatoes makes their flesh especially soft and fluffy, ready for generous smears of tahini butter. Lime juice, soy sauce, and sesame oil make the flavors especially dynamic, and a welcome savory counterpoint to classic sweet potato casserole.

Thin rounds of sweet potato are arranged upright in concentric circles, then roasted with harissa until tender and crisp-edged. A crunchy dukkah of pistachios, sesame, and fennel seeds finishes this striking holiday side.

This gluten-free stuffing skips the usual process of baking cornbread, cubing it, and drying it out. Instead, mushrooms, kale, and herbs bake right into the batter.

Chewy wild rice, tossed with sautéed leeks, toasted pecans, and fresh herbs, makes a stunningly delicious (and gluten-free) alternative to traditional Thanksgiving stuffing.

If you’re firmly Team Dark Meat, these stock-braised turkey legs are the ticket. The meat becomes tender enough to pull from the bone, making for especially good leftover sandwiches the next day.

Prefer white meat, or feeding a smaller crowd? A bone-in turkey breast delivers juicy, flavorful slices without the work of roasting a whole bird. No basting or oversized roasting pan required.

Or give a whole roasted salmon fillet the holiday treatment with a crunchy salsa of toasted nuts, garlic, chile, and vinegar. Showered with fresh mint and cilantro, it’s a striking centerpiece with plenty of protein.

A crisp, golden shell of saffron rice gives way to spiced chickpeas, caramelized onions, and tart dried cherries. Crown the whole thing with a bracingly fresh herb salad for a vegetarian centerpiece everyone will love.

For a meatless main with all the ceremony of a holiday roast, this homemade tofu loaf gets filled with savory mushroom-pecan stuffing and brushed with a smoky maple-soy glaze. Pass the mushroom gravy alongside.

Tearing roasted sweet potatoes into rough chunks creates more surface area for charring and catching a spicy maple-soy glaze. Serve them over tangy lentils with scallions and pistachios for a substantial plant-based main.

A mixture of mushrooms, pearl onions, carrots, and red wine makes a rich, deeply savory vegetarian braise. Serve it over mashed potatoes or polenta, with crispy mushrooms scattered over the top.

Transform humble cabbage into a deeply flavorful vegetarian centerpiece. Here, it caramelizes while slowly braising in a spiced tomato broth. Serve the tender wedges over grains to make the meal more substantial.

Almond flour makes these warmly spiced cake layers exceptionally tender, while shredded carrots, walnuts, golden raisins, and coconut bring texture to every bite. Tangy cream cheese–Greek yogurt frosting seals the deal. Make it up to three days ahead.

Whole wheat flour and oats bring subtle nuttiness to this apple crisp, while brown sugar and butter help the topping turn golden. Serve warm, with vanilla ice cream for anyone who wants it.

This Spanish almond cake gets a seasonal turn with chopped pears and plenty of citrus zest. Naturally gluten-free and dairy-free, it’s lovely after dinner—and just as welcome with coffee the next morning.

Rich chocolate mousse gets a crackly crown of sweet sesame brittle. Serve it in individual glasses for a holiday-party-worthy capper that’s entirely vegan—and a little different from the usual parade of Thanksgiving desserts.

Golden turmeric, fragrant spices, and coconut milk give this custard pie its silky filling. The almond, oat, and coconut crust is naturally gluten-free, making the finished dessert suitable for guests avoiding both gluten and dairy.

A platter of seasonal citrus—think grapefruit, mandarin oranges, and whatever else looks good at the market—gets a crunchy topping of pistachios, almonds, pumpkin seeds, and toasted coconut.

#6519. Mini Pumpkin Pies

Pumpkin pie is a Thanksgiving dinner must-have, but what to do when there are more diners than slices? Or, what if you're more of a crust-lover than filling? Enter these adorable mini pumpkin pies, which rethink the crust-to-filling ratio in the most adorable, snackable package. These mini pies are perfect for people who want just a little treat after the big meal, or if you'd prefer a smattering of desserts, since honestly, who can choose between pumpkin and pecan? No baking experience? No problem. These super-easy pumpkin pies are not just cute, but incredibly easy to make too.

To start, arrange a rack in the center of the oven and preheat it to 375°. As the oven heats, grease the bottoms and sides of a 24-cup mini muffin tin with cooking spray or butter. This will help you get a golden-brown crust that doesn’t stick to the tins.

Transfer the dough rounds into the prepared muffin tin, gently pressing the dough to the bottom and sides of each cup. Once each cup is filled with dough, place the tin into the refrigerator to allow the dough to chill for about 15 minutes.

As the dough chills, whisk the pumpkin puree, condensed milk, egg, vanilla, salt, and baking spices in a large mixing bowl until smooth and well combined.

Remove the muffin tin from the fridge and spoon about 1 heaping tablespoon of filling into each cup. The filling should reach almost all the way up the sides of each mini pie crust.

Place the tin into the oven and bake the pies for about 25 to 30 minutes, until the centers are just set and the edges are golden brown. Remove them from the oven and allow the pies to cool in the tin for 10 minutes before using a small offset spatula or spoon to gently remove the pies from the tin and transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely.

As the pies cool, whip the heavy whipping cream in a large bowl until soft peaks form. Top each of the mini pies with a dollop of fresh whipped cream and, if desired, shave chocolate over the tops. Finally, sprinkle the pies with a bit of cinnamon for an extra seasonal touch.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you want to freeze these pies, let them cool completely, then freeze them on a baking sheet until solid. Transfer to an airtight container once frozen and defrost at room temperature to eat.

#6518. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

How much do you know about our blue planet? Test your terran knowledge with our Earth quiz!

Deepa Jain is a freelance science writer from Bengaluru, India. Her educational background consists of a master's degree in biology from the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and an almost-completed bachelor's degree in archaeology from the University of Leicester, UK. She enjoys writing about astronomy, the natural world and archaeology.
